advertising-e-commerce.problem_shape: These papers share a marketplace problem: a platform must decide what product, ad, price, coupon, page layout, campaign, or answer to put in front of a person while money, attention, trust, and inventory are all limited. A shopping site does not merely retrieve matching items. It has to guess whether a person will click, buy, return, abandon, compare across shops, accept a delivery promise, or be harmed by unsafe advertising. An advertising system has the same pressure with a different surface: it must spend a budget over channels and moments before the final value is fully known. The input evidence shows this pressure across 152 papers, with many examples in WWW and SIGIR and smaller groups in WSDM and KDD. The family belongs together because each paper treats commerce as a repeated allocation problem under partial evidence. The system sees queries, images, catalog fields, prices, bids, clicks, conversions, refunds, seller behavior, ad content, and experiment results, then must turn those fragments into a choice that affects buyers, sellers, advertisers, and the platform.
advertising-e-commerce.naive_failure: A smart beginner would rank by the most obvious signal: show visually similar products for an image query, favor items with many clicks, spend more where recent sales were high, suppress risky results when a model score is low, or trust an A/B test when one version wins. Those rules fail because commerce feedback is delayed, mixed, and shaped by the platform itself. A click can happen long before a purchase, and a purchase can later be refunded. An item-level score can miss the fact that the same product at a different price behaves differently. Popular products and strong sellers get more exposure because they were already exposed. Ads compete for attention beside other ads. A layout change can alter where people look, not just what they prefer. Scam campaigns rotate content and hide behind harmless-looking material. In this family, the simple score is usually too flat for the decision it controls.
advertising-e-commerce.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is controlled decision-making from incomplete feedback. In plain terms, the system builds a score for each possible action, but it also asks what that score is allowed to mean. Conversion papers estimate chances: given this user, item, price, and time, how likely is a click, purchase, refund, delivery delay, or booking? Ranking papers sort candidates, but the order must balance relevance, variety, page position, visual evidence, long-term satisfaction, and business value. Bidding and budget papers choose settings by defining what counts as wrong, such as spending too fast, underspending, violating a coupon constraint, or missing conversions, then adjusting decisions to reduce that wrongness. Causal papers compare like with like so the platform does not confuse a decision that caused a sale with a decision merely shown near a likely sale. Testing papers use repeated experiments to estimate whether a change is real or noise. Safety and anomaly papers compare current content or prediction patterns with expected patterns, then flag sharp departures. The tradeoff is accuracy versus cost, revenue versus user welfare, fast action versus delayed truth, and personalization versus unfair or unsafe exposure.
advertising-e-commerce.why_math_matters: The math matters because online commerce has structure that ordinary rules leave unused. A booking path has stages: a person may search, click, consider substitutes, book, or leave. A campaign has language that may point only indirectly to product types. A product has text, image, brand, price, stock status, seller offers, and sometimes many near-duplicate variants. A budget has time: money spent early cannot be spent later, but waiting too long may miss valuable moments. These structures make the data less like a pile of independent facts and more like a set of connected clocks, funnels, and scarce slots. Probability is useful because final outcomes arrive late and unevenly. Ranking is useful because the platform can show only a few things. Control and planning are useful because bids and budgets must be adjusted while feedback is still arriving. Careful testing is useful because many users and sellers behave differently, and parallel experiments can interfere with each other. The papers need these tools to separate signal from exposure, timing, layout, price, and strategic behavior.
advertising-e-commerce.paper_family: The representative papers are different branches of the same deeper move: make the marketplace choice more faithful before acting on it. CASCADE separates conversion and refund timing instead of pretending net conversion is immediately visible. Price SKU modeling says a product cannot be scored only at item level when price variants change behavior. ARCHER, MMRM, MCRec, catalog-quality work, and campaign-to-product attribution all repair the meaning match between queries, images, brand knowledge, campaigns, covers, and products. STCRank, whole-page search, demand-calibrated facet diversification, and CoCo focus on the order or suppression decision: what should be shown, where, and with how much confidence? DARA, GAM, AHBid, TAR, ZIPBid, and small-budget feedback control treat advertising as a paced sequence of spending choices under constraints. Prediction Guardian, scam-campaign anatomy, unsafe YouTube advertising detection, brand-safety detection, EVADE-Bench, and the hidden energy-cost study add the trust branch: commercial systems must notice corruption, evasion, inappropriate ads, and costs pushed onto users. AgenticShop, ACES, WebMall, Click-to-Ask, and live-shopping assistants show a newer interface where agents and language systems help shop, compare, ask, choose, and sell across marketplaces with live context.
advertising-e-commerce.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is less about a single click predictor and more about commerce systems that must reason across richer surfaces. The evidence shows price-level conversion, refund delay, whole-page layout, spatial ad interactions, multimodal product ranking, live-stream question answering, catalog repair, multi-shop agent evaluation, and agentic buying behavior. Large language models appear often, but mostly as interpreters, planners, assistants, or label builders rather than magic replacements for marketplace measurement. Another shift is operational pressure: budget pacing, real-time anomaly response, parallel experimentation, sparse feedback, thousands of repeated items, and evasive content all force methods to work under deployment constraints. The common change is broader responsibility for the decision loop, from matching and ranking through spending, safety, measurement, and governance.
advertising-e-commerce.limits: The family depends on logged marketplace data being a useful guide to future marketplace behavior. That assumption can fail when past rankings created the evidence, when sellers strategically adapt, when scams change templates, or when an AI shopping agent has different biases from human buyers. Conversion and bidding models can be numerically precise while still optimizing the wrong business or user outcome. A/B tests can reduce false positives, but they do not settle long-term welfare, seller fairness, or effects that spill across experiments. Multimodal and language systems rely on catalog text, images, brand knowledge, and generated labels being accurate enough to trust. The input evidence reports problems, approaches, and contributions, not full deployment proof across all product categories, countries, advertisers, page designs, or adversarial settings.

causal-inference.problem_shape: This family is about systems that must decide what would change if something were acted on, not just what tends to appear beside what. The setting may be travel inventory, marketing subsidies, search-page layout, social A/B tests, recommendation, fact-checking, medical diagnosis, time-series forecasting, graph anomaly detection, or human belief in synthetic content. In each case, a platform sees many signals at once: users, items, prices, histories, graph links, text, images, service indicators, or model answers. Some signals are useful causes, meaning changing them would change the outcome. Others are passengers that only ride along with the true driver. The shared problem is that a wrong cause leads to a wrong intervention. A travel platform may stock the wrong inventory, a recommender may learn popularity instead of preference, a language model may repeat a demographic shortcut, and a social experiment may misread spillover through friendships as a direct treatment result. These papers belong together because they treat prediction as insufficient when the next step is an action, explanation, audit, or policy decision.
causal-inference.naive_failure: A smart beginner would collect past data, find the strongest patterns, and act on them: promote the product linked with higher sales, suppress a poor search result, recommend what similar users clicked, or trust the feature that best predicts a label. That fails because the strongest pattern may be caused by exposure, source bias, missing attributes, network spillover, popularity, familiar fake news, or a shortcut inside a graph. Users who received a subsidy may already have been likely buyers. Items with high clicks may simply have been shown more often. In a social platform test, one treated user can affect an untreated neighbor, so the two groups are no longer cleanly separated. In language and multimodal systems, fluent wording, visual cues, or demographic associations can look predictive while carrying the wrong reason. Acting on these patterns can amplify the mistake that created the data.
causal-inference.mathematical_principle: The central mathematical idea is comparison between worlds that cannot both be observed. For one user, item, page, service, or graph node, we can see what happened under the action actually taken. We cannot directly see what would have happened if the inventory had arrived sooner, the subsidy had been withheld, the page layout had changed, the model had ignored a demographic cue, or a neighbor had not been exposed. Causal inference is the attempt to build that missing comparison carefully. The papers do this by separating possible drivers from misleading companions, balancing groups so compared cases are more alike, estimating treatment effects, tracing mediator steps that carry influence, blocking non-causal paths through graphs, or creating counterfactual examples that ask what should stay the same when only one factor changes. Probability enters because the missing world is uncertain, so the system estimates chances from repeated cases rather than claiming certainty. Graphs enter when influence can travel along links. The recurring tradeoff is actionability versus assumption: the answer is more useful than plain prediction only if the comparison really removes the misleading differences.
causal-inference.why_math_matters: The math matters because these domains have structure that ordinary rules cannot hold in memory. Actions happen inside connected systems. A hotel supply decision can affect platform-wide sales, a search page is a two-dimensional layout rather than a simple list, and a TikTok experiment can leak influence through a learned interference graph. Evidence is also partly hidden. Knowledge graphs may miss attributes, networked people may share unseen factors, and causal discovery may need latent variables, meaning important causes that are not directly recorded. Several papers exploit stability: if a feature keeps helping across sources, domains, subgraphs, or time periods, it is more likely to reflect the thing that actually matters than a local accident. Other papers exploit controlled disruption: change a reasoning trace, augment sentiment text with a counterfactual version, adjust model confidence when outside evidence conflicts with internal belief, or isolate a subgraph explanation and see whether the prediction still follows. This structure lets the papers ask a sharper question than accuracy alone: would changing this chosen piece change the outcome we care about?
causal-inference.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each one repairs a different broken comparison. The travel inventory and marketing subsidy papers ask which business action truly adds sales rather than rewarding customers who would have bought anyway. Whole-page e-commerce search and CoCo ask how to rank or suppress results when position, layout, uncertainty, revenue, profit, and long-term satisfaction can mask the real effect of a decision. TikTok A/B testing and network treatment-effect work handle interference, where one person's treatment changes another person's outcome. Recommendation papers such as C-HyPOD, MCLMR, causal diffusion preference modeling, and neuro-symbolic multi-behavior recommendation separate preference from popularity, sparse history, behavior alignment, or graph shortcuts. Graph papers such as CausalSKyHop, invariant heterogeneous graph learning, BaLu, and heterophilic graph disentanglement ask which links carry explanation and which links spread noise. Language and multimodal papers, including sarcasm understanding, aspect sentiment, fact-checking, biased question answering, and hallucination susceptibility, apply the same logic to words, images, and reasoning traces. The common move is not one method name. It is rebuilding the comparison so an action, explanation, or audit targets a cause rather than a coincidence.
causal-inference.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family spreads causal reasoning into deployed web systems and large pretrained models. The evidence is not only about estimating an effect in a clean table. It includes online travel revenue, e-commerce page layout, TikTok-scale experiments, cold-start recommendation, model-selection tools, fact-checking with conflicting knowledge, medical diagnosis, microservice forecasting, time series, multimodal sarcasm, and knowledge graphs. Another change is the mix of causal thinking with representation learning, meaning compact learned descriptions, and with language models that add semantic clues but can also add overconfidence or bias. The family is also more concerned with stress cases: missing graph attributes, limited labels, changing domains, network spillover, source bias, out-of-distribution recommendation, and fairness after causal pre-training.
causal-inference.limits: These papers depend on assumptions that the input evidence cannot prove by itself. A causal graph may leave out an important hidden cause. A counterfactual example may change more than the intended factor. A stable feature across domains may still be a shared shortcut. Network interference methods need the learned links to match real influence, not just observed contact. Business-effect estimates rely on logging, assignment, and measurement being trustworthy. Language-model interventions assume the edited reasoning trace is tied to the answer in the claimed way. Reported gains, including revenue, GMV, fairness, or robustness gains, do not prove that the same method will transfer across platforms, cultures, time periods, user incentives, or adversarial behavior.

efficiency-scalability.problem_shape: This family is about systems that already know what they would like to do, but cannot afford to do it in the direct way. A recommender could store a rich profile for every user and item. A search system could compare every query with every document. A graph method could inspect every link pattern. A cloud network could shape every traffic flow by hand. These papers start from the same pressure: the useful signal is spread across huge collections, long histories, many users, many documents, many graph links, or many devices, while the service still has to answer quickly and cheaply. The scarce resource changes from paper to paper: memory in sparse recommendation layers, model knobs in vision and language adaptation, retrieval calls in PruneRAG, network capacity in BeeQoS, energy in GreenWebInspector, and time in long-context ranking or graph clustering. The family is not just about making things faster. It is about deciding which detail is worth keeping, which work can be reused, which candidates can be ignored, and which guarantees must survive when the system is made smaller.
efficiency-scalability.naive_failure: A smart beginner would try the most faithful version first: keep all features, train or tune the whole model, scan the whole list, retrieve every possible piece of evidence, enumerate every graph pattern, or allocate network capacity with fixed rules. That works while the example is small, because nothing important is thrown away. It fails when the pile grows. Full tuning of large vision or language models becomes expensive across many tasks. Dense user and item profiles waste memory in production recommendation. Sliding windows for long document ranking repeat work and raise API cost. Random negative examples in biomedical knowledge graphs spend training effort on easy non-links. Static bandwidth shaping cannot follow changing tenants. Exhaustive graph enumeration preserves structure but becomes impractical. The repeated failure is that completeness treats every part as equally worth paying for, even though real data usually has uneven value.
efficiency-scalability.mathematical_principle: The central mathematical idea is controlled approximation: do less work while making an explicit choice about what error, delay, memory use, or unfairness is acceptable. In plain terms, the papers build a price tag for each possible piece of work. A candidate document, graph edge, model parameter, traffic flow, time step, seed URL, or training example is kept when it seems likely to change the answer, and skipped or compressed when it mostly repeats what is already known. Sometimes the price tag is a score, as in confidence-guided query trees or hard negative selection. Sometimes it is a constraint, as in bandwidth guarantees, fair chore allocation, device limits, or privacy-preserving identity. Sometimes it is a compact shape: a sparse user profile, a graph contraction, a shortest path through a knowledge graph, or a linear-time event model that updates a small running state instead of rereading the full past. The tradeoff is always accuracy versus cost, with cost meaning time, memory, network traffic, energy, labels, or human maintenance. The math matters because it turns a vague command like save resources into a repeatable rule for deciding what can be safely ignored.
efficiency-scalability.why_math_matters: Efficiency papers need math because the danger is not merely doing too much work; the danger is saving work in the wrong place. Real systems have structure. User histories contain repeated tastes. Web crawls have seeds with different future yield. Graphs have neighborhoods where nearby nodes carry related evidence, but also noisy links that should be weakened. Long documents have positions where only some passages influence the final order. Cloud traffic has priority classes and changing demand. Time sequences often contain slow patterns that can be tracked without rereading every event. These structures let a system replace brute force with measured shortcuts. Counting-based graph clustering avoids listing every large pattern by estimating enough of the structure to preserve bicliques. Relative position memory in recommendation keeps co-occurrence clues without storing everything. Fourier graph learning treats long-term event patterns as mixtures of slow and fast rhythms, reducing repeated local processing. The rule underneath is: spend computation where the world is irregular, uncertain, or decision-changing, and reuse or shrink where the world is repetitive.
efficiency-scalability.paper_family: The representative papers look different because they save different resources, but they share the same move: preserve the decision signal while cutting waste. Efficient Learning of Sparse Representations from Interactions keeps high-dimensional recommender expressiveness but stores only active pieces, using an inverted-index style lookup so production matching is lighter. Parameter-efficient vision transformer work asks which small parts of a large visual model need changing for a new task, instead of retuning the whole model. LongRanker and PruneRAG both attack repeated retrieval work: one tries to rerank a long list in one pass, while the other expands a reasoning tree only when confidence says more evidence is needed. BeeQoS moves the same idea into cloud networks by separating fast packet handling from demand-aware control. URLBank applies it to crawling by choosing seeds with higher marginal gain. Graph papers such as biclique-preserving clustering, SAGAD, weighted graph contraction, and RAG-GFM reduce the graph or retrieve from it without pretending every edge deserves equal cost. Even GreenWebInspector belongs here: it predicts energy tier from static page features so energy cost can be seen before device-specific measurement.
efficiency-scalability.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is more deployment-shaped. The input file shows efficiency pressure across WWW, SIGIR, WSDM, and KDD, with 657 papers, or 33.9 percent of the collection, and many examples tied to live services: recommendation, web crawling, LLM search engines, cloud bandwidth, customs classification, medical diagnosis, and edge devices. The newer pattern is not just smaller models. It is adaptive thrift: systems decide at run time or update time how much evidence, memory, tuning, routing, or graph detail a particular case deserves. Caching, pruning, sparse storage, shortest paths, compact states, and constraint checks are becoming ordinary parts of the method, not afterthoughts.
efficiency-scalability.limits: These papers depend on the shortcut matching the real source of waste. Sparse profiles help only if most stored dimensions are usually inactive. Graph reduction helps only if removed or reweighted links do not carry rare but crucial evidence. Confidence-guided retrieval can miss facts when early confidence is falsely high. Parameter-efficient tuning can fail when the new task needs changes in parts of the model that were frozen. Energy prediction from static web features may not cover every device or runtime behavior. Bandwidth allocation assumes priorities and demand estimates are trustworthy. The input evidence reports representative gains and guarantees for particular settings, but it does not prove that every shortcut transfers across domains, data sizes, traffic patterns, or user populations.

explainability-interpretability.problem_shape: These papers share a practical pressure: important systems are making decisions that people cannot safely accept as silent guesses. The decision may be whether an image is illegal abuse material, why a social-media post signals humanitarian need, which graph edges can be removed, why a recommendation was made, whether a meme is harmful, why a machine looks anomalous, or which evidence in a hate video supports a label. In each case the output is not enough. A correct-looking answer still leaves the user unable to check whether the system used the right clues, ignored noise, followed domain rules, or broke under small changes. The family is therefore about turning hidden model behavior into inspectable evidence. Some papers expose parts, such as concepts, paths, roles, labels, subgraphs, event interactions, spatial cues, or retrieved facts. Others add interfaces, agents, or reports so a person can question the result. The shared real-world problem is accountability under complexity: when data comes from images, text, graphs, sequences, user histories, auctions, maintenance streams, or counseling dialogue, the system must show what mattered and why.
explainability-interpretability.naive_failure: A smart beginner might try two simple fixes. The first is to use a more accurate model and trust the score. That fails because a high score does not say whether the model relied on a face, a body cue, a graph path, a cultural symbol, a noisy chat turn, or a misleading popular item. The second is to ask the model to explain itself afterward in plain language. That also fails when the explanation is only a story placed on top of the decision. Several papers explicitly worry about explanations that are brittle, disconnected, one-time, or not faithful to the actual behavior. Graph explainers can ignore sign patterns or produce broken subgraphs. Search and dialogue systems can explain noisy context instead of the useful signal. Multimodal classifiers can name the wrong text or image clue. In sensitive settings, a plausible explanation can be worse than none because it creates trust without giving a real way to check the decision.
explainability-interpretability.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is evidence assignment: break a decision into candidate pieces, then estimate which pieces changed the outcome and which pieces merely came along for the ride. The pieces differ by setting. In a graph, they can be edges, paths, node roles, communities, attributes, or relation types. In text and images, they can be words, regions, captions, visual concepts, cultural references, or label-linked fragments. In recommendations, they can be user actions, social subgraphs, popularity signals, causal mediators, or item features. In streams and maintenance, they can be event types, timestamps, interaction patterns, or anomaly causes. The math turns these pieces into things that can be compared, scored, hidden, kept, or removed. Some papers measure contribution by removing or perturbing a part and watching how the answer changes. Some use paths or rules so evidence must form a coherent chain. Some compress the decision into concepts or prototypes so similar cases can share names. Some estimate uncertainty or noise so explanations stay compact without becoming fragile. The central tradeoff is simple explanation versus faithful detail: a useful explanation must be small enough for people to inspect, but not so small that it drops the real cause of the decision.
explainability-interpretability.why_math_matters: The math matters because these systems are built on structured signals, not loose collections of facts. A signed social graph has friendly and hostile links, so an explanation for a link prediction should respect how signs combine along paths. A heterogeneous graph has different kinds of nodes and relations, so noise removal must know which relations mean the same thing and which do not. A crisis post pairs text and image evidence, so a rationale transferred from words to pixels must preserve the reason for the label across modes. A meme can be harmful because of the clash between a picture, a joke, and cultural knowledge, not because one word is toxic. A counseling agent needs stage-consistent reasoning because emotional support changes from exploration to insight to action. These papers use scoring, path constraints, concept grouping, relation-aware denoising, information gain, uncertainty estimates, and rule-like reasoning because the world already has parts and connections. The math gives researchers a way to say what should count as a better explanation: more faithful to the decision, more stable under noise, more compact, more human-queryable, more tied to domain concepts, or more useful for intervention.
explainability-interpretability.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they all replace opaque output with structured evidence. Age classification in child sexual abuse material does this by fusing expert-recognized cues such as face, body proportions, and sexual characteristics instead of leaving the decision inside one end-to-end model. Graph papers form a large branch: Shapley-based sparsification scores edge importance, SGExplainer requires balanced signed paths, GNN Explainers 2.0 asks for layer-wise provenance, robust heterogeneous graph explanations separate relation-aware signal from structural noise, and node role-guided clustering turns changing graph groups into named roles. Language-model papers attack the same hidden-behavior problem in recommendations, counseling, conversational search, SQL checking, auto-bidding, and hate-video analysis by making reasoning, retrieved evidence, labels, reports, or action layers explicit. Multimodal papers add another branch: humanitarian classification transfers rationales from text to images, meme and vaccine-misinformation work grounds labels in cultural or visual concepts, and geo-localization uses spatial semantics to make cross-view matching less mysterious. Recommendation and social papers explain synergistic effects, popularity bias, multi-behavior preference, federated contribution, and influential node groups. Across all branches, the deeper move is the same: expose the path from raw signal to decision.
explainability-interpretability.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is broader than classic feature importance. The evidence shows explanations moving into deployed, mixed-data settings: psychological support, emotional dialogue, predictive maintenance, auto-bidding, federated recommendation, graph foundation models, hate video analysis, medical diagnosis, and misinformation detection. Large language models appear often, but usually as one part of an explanation system rather than as trusted narrators. There is also more attention to robustness: explanations should survive graph perturbations, adversarial retrieval changes, noisy context, out-of-context media, missing modalities, and shifting user behavior. The family is moving from static explanations for a single prediction toward evidence that can be queried, transferred across data types, used for debugging, and tied to decisions people must act on.
explainability-interpretability.limits: These outputs depend on assumptions that the input evidence cannot fully prove. An explanation is useful only if the exposed pieces really caused the decision, not merely matched a human-friendly story. Concept-based methods assume the chosen concepts cover the important cues. Graph explanations assume links, signs, roles, and relation types carry real meaning rather than noise or historical bias. Multimodal rationales assume text and image clues can be aligned without losing culture-specific meaning. Agent explanations assume the visible reasoning steps reflect the system's actual choice process. Compact explanations can hide secondary causes, while detailed explanations can overwhelm users. The evidence here reports problems, approaches, and selected contributions; it does not establish that these methods remain faithful across platforms, cultures, adversarial settings, medical contexts, legal review, or future data shifts.

fairness-bias-responsible-ai.problem_shape: This family is about systems that decide who gets seen, believed, recommended, classified, protected, or helped, when the data already carries uneven history. The setting may be a recommender that keeps showing popular items, a search system that ranks political or gendered results, a language model judging toxic speech, a graph model using social links, a vision model trained from web images, or a tool used in crisis response. The shared pressure is that a technical score becomes a real allocation: attention, safety, opportunity, moderation, expert matching, citation credit, data value, or price-consistent exposure. These papers treat unfairness as more than bad manners in a model. It is a measurement problem, because the system must notice which groups, items, regions, cultures, or rare cases are losing. It is also an intervention problem, because the system must change rankings, training data, prompts, features, or evidence flow without destroying usefulness. The family belongs together because every paper asks the same practical question: how can an automated system reuse past patterns without making past imbalance look like neutral evidence?
fairness-bias-responsible-ai.naive_failure: A smart beginner would first train on all available data, measure average accuracy, then add a simple rule such as showing more rare items or equalizing one group count. That can help in a toy case, but it breaks across this family. The data may not say which attributes are sensitive, as in ranking work that avoids protected labels. Bias can hide inside popularity, price granularity, language, culture, skin-tone emoji meaning, graph links, image backgrounds, or transferred knowledge from another domain. Fixing one group can leave another group harmed, which is why multi-attribute graph fairness appears. A simple rule also cannot tell whether an error is caused by missing evidence, historical underexposure, a misleading shortcut, or a changing user setting. Worse, a fairness fix can reduce utility if it blindly removes useful signal, and it can create false confidence if the evaluation only covers the easiest culture, language, platform, or item type.
fairness-bias-responsible-ai.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is constrained comparison. First the system defines what it is trying to compare: users with items, queries with documents, images with labels, locations with text mentions, teams with skills, model answers with toxicity labels, or groups with outcomes. Then it measures both usefulness and unfair imbalance. Usefulness may mean a correct class, a better rank, a good conversion estimate, a reliable geocode, or a helpful recommendation. Imbalance may mean one group receives less exposure, one culture is misread more often, one skin tone is assigned a different sentiment, one citation group is overlooked, or rare classes get weak confidence. The hard part is that both numbers matter at once. Some papers change the data before learning, as FairData and BiasEdit do. Some change the model's inner signals or small added controls, as MultiFPT, FairGE, FairFS, FairSpec, and neuron steering do. Some change decisions after training, as LAFB, FUDLR, FairToT, and fair reranking do. Others audit with causal, economic, graph, or benchmark views. In plain terms, the math turns fairness into a set of comparisons and limits, then searches for decisions that stay useful while reducing measured harm.
fairness-bias-responsible-ai.why_math_matters: The math matters because unfairness often rides on ordinary predictive structure. Popular items really do have more clicks, familiar videos really may be easier to watch, prestigious institutions really do sit in dense citation networks, and majority-language data really is easier for a model to learn from. A hand-written rule cannot simply delete those signals, because some of them are useful. The papers need measurement tools that separate helpful evidence from shortcuts that only reflect unequal exposure. Graph methods use the fact that neighbors carry information, but add checks because links can also carry social bias. Causal evaluation asks whether two patterns merely appear together or whether changing one would change the outcome. Privacy-preserving data trading adds carefully shared noise, meaning random masking that hides individual information while preserving enough total signal to price or use data. Ranking and recommendation papers define tradeoffs between accuracy, exposure, novelty, and fairness. The common structure is balance under uncertainty: keep the signal that helps the task, weaken the signal that mainly repeats historical advantage, and state which groups or outcomes define that balance.
fairness-bias-responsible-ai.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each locates bias in a different part of the same decision chain. FairLRM, FUDLR, FairSpec, neuron steering, LAFB, and cross-domain recommendation papers focus on recommenders, where popularity, familiarity, transferred knowledge, or language-model pretraining can over-serve already visible items or users. Refairmulate, FAIR-RAG, responsible retrieval perspectives, and trustworthy personalized retrieval move the same concern into search and generated answers: the system must choose evidence and wording without leaning one political, gendered, private, or culturally narrow way. MultiFPT, FairGE, OpeNTF2, graph classification, citation disparity, and fair streaming clustering show the graph version of the problem, where links and centers spread opportunity as well as information. BiasEdit, skin-tone emoji analysis, hateful meme evaluation, and motion-metric work ask whether visual or multimodal systems are judging the right object rather than a biased shortcut. ARC, TabPFN fairness evaluation, social bias benchmark reviews, and responsible prompting are auditing branches: they build tests, rubrics, or tools for deciding when a model is trustworthy enough to use. Across all branches, the deeper move is the same: expose the hidden comparison, measure who loses, then alter data, ranking, routing, prompts, or evaluation so the loss is no longer invisible.
fairness-bias-responsible-ai.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is shaped by large pretrained systems moving into everyday decision pipelines. Many papers no longer assume that fairness can be fixed only by retraining a whole model. They try lighter interventions: prompt tuning, small adapters, inference-time reassessment, machine unlearning, post-ranking factors, neuron steering, and data editing. The family also widens the target of fairness. It covers culture in hateful memes, geography in humanitarian extraction, political stance in retrieval-augmented answers, skin tone in emoji meanings, multi-attribute graph users, price-level e-commerce decisions, and long-tailed graph classes. Another change is operational seriousness: papers discuss web tools, deployed video recommendation, privacy-preserving markets, expert-team formation, and evaluation protocols, not only clean offline fairness scores.
fairness-bias-responsible-ai.limits: These papers depend on fairness definitions that must be chosen before the system can optimize for them. Equal exposure, equal error rates, better rare-item visibility, safer moderation, cultural balance, privacy, and economic fairness are related but not identical goals. The input evidence reports approaches and selected gains, but not proof that each method transfers across platforms, languages, cultures, time periods, or business incentives. Some methods need reliable group labels or useful proxies; others avoid those labels but may miss hidden harm. Graph links, generated data, edited images, prompts, and benchmark labels can all encode the same bias they are meant to repair. Fairness improvements also depend on user behavior after deployment, because changing what a system shows changes the next data it learns from.

fraud-anomaly-detection.problem_shape: This family is about systems that must notice when behavior stops fitting the world it claims to belong to. The object may be a bank transfer, blockchain wallet, web account, system log, microservice trace, sensor stream, advertising prediction, vehicle signal, pathology image, fake-news post, video scene, or tool call made by an agent. The shared real-world task is not simply to catch rare cases. It is to decide what ordinary behavior means when ordinary itself is moving, incomplete, and sometimes deliberately copied by attackers. Fraudsters imitate normal users. Broken services produce bursts and irregular gaps. Laundered money moves through shallow transfer structures. Poisoned tools or federated updates may look legitimate until their downstream effect appears. Many papers therefore treat anomaly detection as a comparison problem under uncertainty: compare an account with its own sequence, a graph object with its neighborhood, a stream with its recent rhythm, or a prediction distribution with the expected pattern. The family exists because modern web and finance systems are too large, fast, and connected for manual rule lists, while false alarms are costly and missed attacks can spread.
fraud-anomaly-detection.naive_failure: A smart beginner would write rules for known bad signs: flag unusually large payments, too many transfers, strange log messages, dense suspicious neighborhoods, or predictions that cross a fixed threshold. That works for clean and stable cases. It fails in the evidence here because the abnormal case often hides inside normal-looking surface behavior. Illicit accounts can use the same actions as ordinary users but in different contexts. Finance fraud appears in sparse graphs and across networks whose habits differ. Graph-level detection cannot assume the training pile is clean, because abnormal graphs may already be mixed in. Streams drift, so yesterday's normal may be today's false alarm. Fake media campaigns scale by reusing templates and cloaking them with harmless-looking content. A second beginner move is to ask for more labels, but many settings have few labels, sensitive data, or no reliable fraud examples. The repeated failure is treating normal as fixed, labeled, and obvious.
fraud-anomaly-detection.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is measured surprise. First the system builds a description of expected behavior from repeated cases: common action orders, usual transaction paths, normal graph neighborhoods, typical time rhythms, ordinary prediction score patterns, or familiar combinations of text, image, and structure. Then a new case is compared against that description. The comparison may use closeness, where a case is suspicious if its nearest neighbors are unlike it; density, where sparse regions of the learned pattern map are treated as risky; sequence fit, where actions are judged by their order and context; graph evidence, where nodes, links, communities, and subgraphs all contribute; or chance estimates, where the system asks how plausible a value is given recent history. Some papers also create controlled abnormal examples so a model can learn what separation should look like when real labels are scarce. Others use a repeated adjustment process: define what counts as a bad separation between normal and abnormal, then change the model to reduce that wrongness. The tradeoff is sensitivity versus false alarms, local detail versus shared pattern, speed versus completeness, and detection strength versus privacy or deployment cost.
fraud-anomaly-detection.why_math_matters: The math matters because abnormal behavior is usually relational, not isolated. A single Ethereum transfer may look ordinary, but a fast chain of shallow transfers after an exploit is a laundering clue. A single log line may not diagnose a microservice failure, but irregular timing, bursts, and relations among log types can. A user action can be harmless in one sequence and suspicious in another. A graph neighbor can help when linked objects share behavior, but can mislead when fraud deliberately attaches itself to normal accounts or when connected nodes are unlike each other. Time methods matter because streams change; the detector must update the expected pattern without forgetting rare warnings. Multi-source methods matter because finance, pathology, vehicles, fake news, and video threats often need text, visual, temporal, and structural clues to agree. The papers need measured comparison because hand rules cannot say how much mismatch is enough, which source deserves trust, or when a strange case is new fraud rather than harmless novelty.
fraud-anomaly-detection.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each one repairs a different weak definition of normal. Pattern-aware illicit account detection studies action order and context, because the same click or transfer can mean different things inside different behavior stories. F2-Gen tackles the missing-data branch by generating scenario-driven financial transactions and graphs when real bank data cannot be shared. The fully unsupervised graph anomaly work and G-GLAD both reject the clean-training assumption, asking how to learn when normal and abnormal are mixed or when labeled abnormal graphs are too narrow. MOE-GTL, heterogeneous graph alignment, DyConAD, SAGAD, PAGE, subgraph anomaly work, graph foundation modeling, and tabular foundation models for graph detection all treat graph structure as evidence that must be aligned, transferred, flattened, expanded, or filtered. TraceLLM, DyLogNet, Smart Eye, and ECLAD apply the same family logic to logs, traces, and maintenance, where the output must be fast and explainable. Prediction Guardian monitors advertising score patterns for silent corruption. Ethereum laundering, federated knowledge-graph poisoning, MCP tool poisoning, CLARF, ProvGuard, CEAT, and Deception Factories form the adversarial branch: the abnormal case is strategically shaped to pass as normal.
fraud-anomaly-detection.what_changed: The 2026 version is less about one fraud classifier and more about anomaly detection as an operating layer across web infrastructure, finance, media, sensors, agents, and graphs. The input file lists 72 papers, mostly from WWW 2026, with SIGIR, WSDM, and KDD also present. The newer pressure is messy deployment: few labels, mixed normal and abnormal training data, changing streams, sparse and heterogeneous graphs, cross-network transfer, privacy limits, latency limits, and attackers who poison tools, federated updates, media templates, or emotional cues. Large language models appear as log analysts, trace readers, explanation agents, or pattern proposers, but the evidence still centers on controlled comparison and verification rather than free-form text generation.
fraud-anomaly-detection.limits: These papers assume that the chosen evidence actually separates harmful novelty from harmless difference. That can fail when attackers copy the measured pattern, when unusual but legitimate users live in sparse regions, or when a graph link carries the wrong meaning. Stream methods assume recent history is still a useful guide after drift. Transfer methods assume different chains, networks, or domains share enough structure to borrow from one another. Synthetic fraud data helps reproducibility only if its scenarios resemble real financial behavior. Explanation tools can make alerts easier to inspect, but the input evidence does not prove that operators will act correctly. The evidence reports claimed problems, approaches, and selected gains, not full proof across all platforms, adversaries, languages, devices, or deployment conditions.

generative-diffusion.problem_shape: These papers share one pressure: many systems now need to create a useful missing thing, not only choose from things already present. The missing thing may be an image with a hidden watermark, a building layout from rough language, a molecule with desired properties, a dense travel path from sparse GPS points, a synthetic fraud pattern that preserves memory without storing real transactions, a graph for agents to work together, or a ranked list shaped around a user's next likely action. The family exists because the real world gives partial, noisy, and conflicting evidence. A user history is sparse, a web answer may contain conflict, a sensor path has gaps, a private client cannot share all data, and a molecule must satisfy several conditions at once. Generation here means filling a gap while obeying constraints. Diffusion-style work appears because many of these gaps are too structured for one-shot guessing. The papers repeatedly ask how to start from uncertainty, add guidance, remove noise, and end with an object that still fits the task.
generative-diffusion.naive_failure: A smart beginner might try direct construction: read the request, predict the final item, and check whether it looks plausible. For recommendations, that means scoring items from past clicks. For molecules, it means searching for structures with the target properties. For trajectories, it means connecting observed GPS points with simple interpolation. For fraud, it means saving old examples for replay. For conflicting web evidence, it means attaching retrieved text and asking a model to answer. These simple moves fail because the missing object must satisfy several linked conditions at once. Local fixes can break global shape: a molecule can meet one property while violating another, a route can pass through impossible movements, a watermark can survive attacks while damaging image quality, and synthetic replay can preserve old fraud labels while losing graph relationships. Direct guessing also handles uncertainty poorly. It gives one answer without showing how noise was removed or which constraints shaped the result.
generative-diffusion.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is gradual repair. Instead of jumping straight to the final object, the system treats generation as a path from messy uncertainty toward a structured answer. In a diffusion model, the everyday picture is this: take an object, learn how it gets corrupted by added noise, then learn the reverse skill of removing that noise step by step. That reverse path gives the model many chances to use conditions, such as a desired molecular property, a user preference, a graph relation, a frequency pattern, a budget limit, or a hidden watermark strength. Flow matching uses a related idea: learn how to move a cloud of simple starting points into the shape of valid final objects. Graph methods add another layer: the object is made of nodes and links, so repair must preserve which parts are connected and what information should travel along those links. Ranking and control papers define what counts as a better final choice, then adjust generation to reduce the specific kind of wrongness. The tradeoff is control versus variety: too little guidance gives fluent noise, while too much guidance can erase diversity or distort the object.
generative-diffusion.why_math_matters: The math matters because these tasks have hidden shape. A polymer is not a bag of atoms; small structural changes can alter several properties together. An antibody is not just a sequence; its binding region must fit an antigen surface in three-dimensional geometry. A user's behavior is not one preference; it changes across actions, time, and item types. A transaction stream is not a set of isolated records; fraud evidence lives in changing links among accounts, merchants, times, and amounts. A QR code must still scan while carrying compressed visual meaning. These structures make hand-written rules brittle. Gradual denoising gives the system a way to test and correct the object repeatedly while using the available condition at each step. Graph-based generation lets evidence move through neighbors rather than treating every part alone. Constraint-based planning lets advertising and marketing papers balance budget, coupons, channels, and business goals. The key advantage is that the papers can define what must be preserved, what may change, and what kind of error matters for the setting.
generative-diffusion.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they use generation as controlled completion under pressure. Molecular papers such as Graph Diffusion Evolution Model and AbFlow complete chemical or antibody structures while obeying property and geometric conditions. TRACE and FSDI fill missing time-series or movement values, but they preserve state changes or frequency energy instead of drawing a smooth line through gaps. STG-DGR and CeFGC generate synthetic graph examples so a system can remember fraud patterns or share knowledge across clients without moving all raw data. Recommendation papers such as GSDiffRec, latent preference diffusion, semantic diffusion, rationale-first graph generation, and semantic IDs use generated preference or item structure to repair sparse, noisy, or inefficient comparison. AHBid and GAM turn generation toward action: they produce plans for bidding, coupons, or channel allocation while respecting constraints. Lang2Plan, OFA-MAS, and Unicoon generate layouts, agent collaboration graphs, or social simulations where the output is a structured world. Conflict-aware retrieval, logical denoising, conditional extraction, watermarking, steganographic QR codes, fake-news generation, scam-campaign analysis, and model-card generation show the same logic for trust: generate or clean information only after deciding which signals should control the result.
generative-diffusion.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that generative work is moving beyond making realistic samples. The evidence shows generation being used as an operational tool for repair, memory, compression, planning, privacy, and control. Diffusion appears in recommendations, fraud streams, federated graphs, time-series imputation, QR compression, advertising bids, molecular design, and knowledge extraction, not only in images. Large language models also appear as controllers, describers, or risk sources around generative systems: they infer user interests, decompose layout requests, simulate information cocoons, create misinformation, or help document AI systems. The center has shifted from can a model make something to can it make the right thing while respecting evidence, constraints, cost, and trust.
generative-diffusion.limits: This family depends on the conditions being real guides rather than decorative labels. If user histories are distorted by past recommendations, generated preferences can repeat that distortion. If graph links are noisy, denoising can spread the wrong evidence. If molecular, antibody, or layout scores only approximate real-world use, the generated object may satisfy the model while failing outside it. Synthetic replay and federated generation reduce storage or communication, but they do not prove privacy by themselves. Watermarks, scam detection, misinformation studies, and QR hiding also face adversaries who adapt. The input evidence gives problems, approaches, and claimed contributions, not full experimental proof, so the family explanation shows the shared logic rather than guaranteeing that each method works across deployments.

graph-learning-mining.problem_shape: This family is about things whose meaning comes from their connections. A node may be a patent, molecule, medical fact, user session, blockchain wallet, telecom opinion, microservice indicator, sketch detail, graph-shaped question, or financial event. A link may mean citation, chemical bond, disease relation, item sequence, money movement, service dependency, shared topic, spatial closeness, or social influence. The shared problem is that the answer is rarely inside one item by itself. Fraud may appear in how accounts move across networks. A medical answer may be safer when it follows disease facts. A graph-level label may depend on rare expert evidence, not the majority class. A recommendation may need user intent that is only visible through item links. These papers ask how to carry useful evidence through links without letting the links overwhelm the original facts. The difficulty is that graphs are not one kind of object. Some connect similar things, some connect opposites, some change over time, some are sparse, some are huge, and some hide sensitive or strategic behavior.
graph-learning-mining.naive_failure: A smart beginner would first flatten the graph into a table: count neighbors, count paths, average nearby features, rank highly connected nodes, or retrieve the closest facts. That can work when links are clean and when connected items really should resemble each other. The input evidence shows why this simple move fails. Topology-aware feature sorting is motivated by graphs where neighbors can be unlike each other, so averaging neighbors washes out the very signal needed. Same-last-item session recommendation shows that two sessions ending with the same item can still reflect different intentions. Random negative examples in biomedical knowledge graphs waste effort because not every false edge is equally informative. Graph anomaly detection cannot assume training data is clean. Large knowledge graphs make exhaustive rule mining too slow. Dynamic event prediction and microservice forecasting need time and dependency structure together, so static counts miss long-range patterns and changing causes.
graph-learning-mining.mathematical_principle: The central mathematical idea is controlled evidence movement. First, the system decides what the objects are and what each link is allowed to mean. Then it turns each object into a compact set of signals, which may include text, time, visual clues, relation type, class evidence, or neighborhood shape. The graph machinery compares nearby and faraway items, decides which neighbors are useful, and limits how much uncertain evidence should travel. In clustering papers, the question is which items belong together when structure and meaning disagree. In retrieval papers, the question is which paths or facts should be selected from a large graph for answering. In anomaly and fraud papers, the question is which pattern is unlikely given its surrounding behavior. In transfer and pre-training papers, the question is which graph habits can carry from one domain to another without copying domain-specific noise. Approximation and sampling appear when the full set of paths or rules is too large to inspect directly. The recurring tradeoff is local detail versus global pattern: follow links enough to use the network, but not so much that rare classes, changing relations, privacy constraints, or opposite-type neighbors disappear.
graph-learning-mining.why_math_matters: The math is necessary because graph evidence creates many competing explanations at once. In a patent system, citation links, technology classes, semantic descriptions, and trend signals can point in different directions. In medical question answering, a language model may produce fluent text, but the disease graph gives a separate test of whether the answer follows known relations. In blockchain fraud, graph links, transaction timing, and text or other modes may each be weak alone but useful when aligned. In molecular editing, the requested edit must respect structure-property relations that may hold outside the examples seen during training. These problems need more than rules such as "trust the nearest neighbor" or "pick the most common label." Mathematical scoring lets a system state what counts as a better grouping, safer answer, more diverse retrieval set, smaller preserved graph, or more believable anomaly warning. It also exposes costs: speed versus completeness in MiniAMIE, compactness versus direction preservation in Dir-GD, diversity versus focus in graph retrieval, and fairness or privacy versus raw prediction in graph fairness and verification work.
graph-learning-mining.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each one changes how evidence is allowed to move through a graph. MiniAMIE restricts the search language and approximates rule scores so large knowledge graphs can be mined quickly. TARD diversifies graph retrieval by using multiple topic-based intents, because one route through a knowledge graph can miss complementary facts needed for question answering. RPO-RAG keeps the same family logic for small language models, aligning retrieved relation paths with answer quality. Structure-Semantic Synergized Deep Contrastive Graph Clustering and LEDA both ask how structure and meaning should be aligned when graphs come from different domains or contain unreliable examples. Topology-aware feature sorting directly challenges the assumption that neighbors are always similar. GraphEVER, graph anomaly detection, and cross-type heterogeneous anomaly work treat uncertainty as part of the answer, especially under rare classes or mixed normal and abnormal data. Dir-GD and network dismantling focus on scale: preserve the important directed or connectivity structure while saving memory or computation. PatentMerit, telecom opinion graph construction, medical graph-constrained answering, and ConceptFormer show the same pattern in language-heavy settings, where text needs graph grounding instead of free-form guesswork.
graph-learning-mining.what_changed: The 2026 version of graph learning is less centered on a single clean graph and more on graphs attached to messy products: finance fraud, telecom opinions, patents, medical answers, recommendations, sketches, microservices, molecules, simulations, and blockchains. The evidence repeatedly points to mixed inputs, cross-domain transfer, long-tailed labels, unclean training data, dynamic behavior, large-scale compression, and safety checks. Language models also appear as graph builders, graph users, and graph-grounded answer generators. Another change is that reliability is part of the task, not an afterthought: papers mention uncertainty, poisoning, fairness, verification, hallucination reduction, interpretability, and structural noise. Scale matters too, with million-level networks and compact substitutes appearing in the evidence.
graph-learning-mining.limits: This family only rests on the input metadata and current repo data, not on full paper proofs or independent replication. The evidence says what the papers claim to address, but not whether the gains hold across unseen platforms, languages, graph sizes, or adversaries. Graph methods break when links encode the wrong relation, when missing edges are not random, when similar-looking neighborhoods hide different causes, or when users and attackers adapt. Transfer claims require source and target graphs to share some reusable structure. Safety and fairness claims depend on which harms are measured. Compression and approximation can preserve headline quality while losing rare but important details.

information-retrieval-search.problem_shape: This family is about finding the few pieces of information that can actually help a person, system, or language model act, while ignoring a huge amount of nearby but unhelpful material. The same shape appears in web search, podcast search, legal case search, formula search, expert finding, crawling, scientific fact-checking, and retrieval-augmented generation, where a model answers by first fetching outside evidence. The real object is not just a document. It may be a passage, a transcript, an email, a product image, a graph neighborhood, a weather archive item, a web page seed, or a standards discussion. The pressure is that the need is often underspecified, the collection is noisy, and the cost of looking everywhere is too high. A search system must turn a vague request into a small ordered set that is useful now. In 2026, these papers also ask whether the returned evidence is explicit, private, fair, safe, multilingual, current, and usable by an answering or acting system.
information-retrieval-search.naive_failure: A smart beginner would first match the words in the request to the words in the collection, then return the items with the most overlap. That works when the user asks for the same words that appear in the right document. It fails when meaning crosses surface form: a legal query may be short while the useful case is long, a Marathi local need may not match translated global wording, a podcast transcript may contain speech errors, and a formula may be easier to recognize visually than by text. The beginner might then rank by general popularity or by whatever an answer model prefers. That fails too, because popular pages can be manipulated, harmful documents can rise during reranking, conflicting sources can sound equally plausible, and personal emails or sensitive data require more than relevance alone. The simple rule sees matching, but not intent, risk, evidence quality, or constraints.
information-retrieval-search.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is to turn search into controlled comparison and ordering under uncertainty. Each candidate item receives signals: word overlap, meaning similarity, source quality, time, language, topic, sensitivity, graph position, expected new information, or risk. The system then balances these signals to choose a small set and an order. In plain terms, it asks: which item is close enough to the need, different enough from the other chosen items, trustworthy enough to cite, cheap enough to fetch, and safe enough to show? Some papers measure top-heavy ranking, where mistakes near the first results matter more because users look there first. Others estimate uncertainty, so a fact-checking system searches the web only when its current evidence is shaky. Graph retrieval treats documents or chunks as connected objects and lets links suggest which neighbors may carry supporting evidence. Crawling work estimates marginal gain, meaning how much extra coverage one more seed is likely to add. Evaluation papers add another layer by measuring how confident we should be when judgments are incomplete. The tradeoff is always speed versus completeness, relevance versus risk, and compact evidence versus lost context.
information-retrieval-search.why_math_matters: The math matters because information collections have structure that hand-written rules cannot track at this scale. Related items cluster by topic, language, visual form, citation, link, conversation turn, or shared evidence chain. Users also create structure: they reformulate queries, switch between name and topic search, judge only a small part of a ranked list, and abandon results when early ranks fail. These patterns are repeated enough that a system can learn useful comparisons, but irregular enough that a fixed checklist breaks. Rank-biased measurement exploits the fact that early positions carry more user attention. Multi-intent graph retrieval exploits the fact that one question may need several complementary neighborhoods, not one best match. Sensitivity-aware search exploits the difference between useful evidence and private exposure. Conflict-aware and risk-aware retrieval exploit the fact that more retrieved text is not always better; some text contradicts, distracts, or harms the answer. The papers need mathematical scoring because the system must make many small tradeoffs consistently, not just declare a page relevant or irrelevant.
information-retrieval-search.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each repairs a different failure in the act of choosing evidence. NeocorRAG and Conflict-Aware RAG focus on answer systems: they do not only fetch passages, they ask whether the passages form explicit evidence chains or contain conflicts that could mislead generation. Risk-aware reranking makes the same point from another angle: a reranker can raise useful documents while also raising harmful ones, so the order must price risk. Multilingual retrieval, Nepali retrieval, Marathi web retrieval, and offline Namibian school search show that access breaks when the collection, language, or infrastructure assumed by mainstream search is missing. Podcast search, MathMex-PDF, legal case retrieval, and multimodal document research show that the object being searched is no longer plain web text; speech, formulas, figures, tables, and long cases need different ways to represent what matters. User simulators and expert-search studies examine the person behind the query, including session changes and mode switching. Privacy-preserving and sensitivity-aware retrieval add a second goal: the system must retrieve without exposing what should remain hidden. URLBank moves the same logic upstream, deciding which web locations are worth collecting before ranking can even happen.
information-retrieval-search.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is less about returning ten blue links and more about supplying evidence to systems that answer, reason, or act. That shift raises the standard: evidence must be explicit enough for reasoning, diverse enough to cover multiple intents, and checked for conflict, harm, privacy, fairness, and source quality. The collection has also widened. Papers cover low-resource languages, offline schools, podcasts, visual math, historical weather archives, climate evidence, security rules, product images, and standards discussions. Evaluation is changing with it: researchers are building new test collections, simulators, and top-weighted measures because old relevance judgments do not capture trust, sensitivity, multilingual access, or multi-step sessions.
information-retrieval-search.limits: These papers assume that the available signals still point toward useful information. That can fail when transcripts are wrong, low-resource collections are sparse, old archives are noisy, web pages are manipulated, or sensitive labels miss what a real person would protect. Many benchmarks and workshops define needed directions, but they do not prove that deployed systems will behave well under changing users, adversarial content, or costly infrastructure. Evidence-chain and conflict methods depend on the retrieved material containing enough truth to compare. Graph and multimodal methods depend on links, chunks, images, formulas, or tables being parsed correctly. Fairness and privacy work also depends on deciding whose harm counts. The family reduces search failure, but it cannot remove the need for careful judgment about evidence, access, and risk.

knowledge-graphs.problem_shape: This family is about systems that need facts to be connected, not just stored. A knowledge graph is a map of things and relations: a person works for an organization, a chemical has a property, a product belongs to a category, a medical answer follows a disease relation, or an event changes another event. The shared real-world problem is that many tasks need this connected map to answer questions, recommend items, detect fraud, verify claims, monitor contaminants, or explain a model decision. A single document, image, table, or transaction often gives only a fragment. The useful evidence sits in paths, neighborhoods, relation types, time changes, and missing links. The input evidence shows 123 papers across WWW, SIGIR, WSDM, and KDD using graphs for question answering, recommendation, fraud detection, scientific extraction, dynamic crawling, fact checking, table search, scene reasoning, and graph generation. They belong together because each paper asks how to turn scattered facts into a structure where evidence can be followed, checked, completed, updated, or protected.
knowledge-graphs.naive_failure: A smart beginner would first make a simple fact table or a simple set of links, then search it directly. For a question, fetch the nearest facts. For recommendation, connect users to liked items. For extraction, ask a language model to list entities and properties. For completion, predict the missing edge that looks most similar to known edges. This breaks because knowledge graphs are incomplete, noisy, and uneven. A shortest path may be cheap but miss the meaning of the relation. A language model may write a fluent property that is inconsistent with the graph. A graph for medicine or fact checking can be dangerous when a missing or poisoned subgraph looks authoritative. Multimodal graphs add another failure: text, images, and structure may disagree. Dynamic graphs add time, so yesterday's map may forget new facts or overwrite old ones.
knowledge-graphs.mathematical_principle: The central mathematical idea is structured evidence movement. The system first decides what counts as an object, what counts as a relation, and what information is allowed to travel across a relation. Then it scores possible paths, neighbors, missing links, extracted properties, or candidate answers by asking whether they fit both the local facts and the wider map. In plain language, a relation is not just a line; it is a claim about how two things should constrain each other. If a drug treats a disease, nearby medical facts can support an answer, but only if the path follows medically meaningful steps. If a user likes an item, item-side facts can help recommendation, but user-side scarcity and noisy links must be handled. If a claim has sub-claims, the graph can schedule which dependency to verify first. Some papers compare paths, some estimate confidence, some generate plausible missing structure, some mine rules, and some compress or profile the graph. The tradeoff is link-following versus link-skepticism: use the map enough to combine evidence, but not so much that wrong, missing, stale, or attacker-made links control the answer.
knowledge-graphs.why_math_matters: The math matters because connected facts create more possibilities than a person can safely handle by rules. A question over a large graph may have many possible paths; S-Path-RAG treats path choice as a measured search so the answer system does not spend words on irrelevant routes. HyperRAG changes the shape of the map when a fact involves more than two things, because splitting one complex fact into pairs can make reasoning drift. Calibration work asks when an answer should be less confident because the retrieved subgraph is incomplete or unreliable. Rule mining such as MiniAMIE needs shortcuts because checking every possible rule in a large graph costs too much time. Multimodal papers need scoring because images, text, and relation structure are useful in different amounts for different relations. The world structure being exploited is that facts constrain one another: related objects make some answers more believable and others less believable. The same structure can mislead when links are copied, stale, sparse, poisoned, or too coarse.
knowledge-graphs.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they all repair the same weak point: useful knowledge is scattered across linked evidence, and the system must decide which links deserve trust. RPO-RAG, GCA-KBQA, S-Path-RAG, HyperRAG, and the unified graph answer systems use relation paths to make question answering more grounded than free-form text generation. AID uses hypothesis subgraphs for conversational recommendation, asking clarifying questions only while several interpretations remain plausible. Knowledge-aware recommendation papers such as SEDIRec, the graph editing model, and spectral heterogeneous diffusion try to clean or enrich item and user evidence before ranking products. LOPE, document-to-graph work, and CompTox ontology construction focus on building consistent maps from scientific, web, or environmental information. DSTAG, continual knowledge graph learning, MetriKG, and dynamic crawling treat knowledge as changing over time rather than fixed. KEPo and poisoning work expose the hostile version of the same design: if attackers can alter graph evolution paths, linked evidence can make a language model confidently wrong. CausalSKyHop, causal knowledge graph papers, and fact-checking work use graphs to show which connected pieces explain, depend on, verify, or constrain others.
knowledge-graphs.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family looks less like storing clean triples and more like running knowledge graphs inside messy systems. The evidence shows graphs tied to small language models, answer generation, fact checking, recommendation, finance fraud, table search, web crawling, 3D scene reasoning, biomedical edge classification, environmental monitoring, and multimodal reasoning. Language models appear as builders, users, and checkers of graphs, but the papers repeatedly add structure around them so fluent text does not replace verification. Another change is trust pressure: calibration, poisoning attacks, safe medical question answering, consistent extraction, dynamic updates, and profiling all treat graph quality as part of the task. Scale also matters, with fast rule mining, synthetic graph generation, and efficient path selection appearing as practical needs.
knowledge-graphs.limits: These explanations rest on the input metadata and current repo JSON, not full paper bodies or independent results. The family assumes that graph links carry meaningful evidence, relation labels are reliable enough, and missing data is not hiding the crucial path. Those assumptions can fail in sparse user graphs, noisy scientific extraction, changing web data, or adversarial GraphRAG settings. Multimodal methods need text, image, and structure to describe compatible facts; otherwise fusion can join signals that should stay separate. Confidence and causal claims depend on whether the graph actually contains the needed alternatives and dependencies. Speedups and synthetic graphs may preserve common structure while losing rare facts. The evidence describes claimed problems and contributions, but does not prove deployment reliability across domains, languages, graph sizes, or attackers.

llm-agents-tool-use.problem_shape: This family is about turning a language model from a talker into a worker. The real object is not just an answer in a chat box. It is a chain of actions: choosing a search tool, calling a ranker, reading a database schema, using memory from earlier sessions, asking another agent to review a plan, or deciding that a simple question should not spend much computing power. The input file shows this across shopping, search, machine-learning workflow construction, book finding, mobile control, software development, emotional support, policy simulation, content moderation, and privacy-literacy tools. The shared pressure is that real tasks sit outside the model. Useful facts live in documents, web pages, tools, databases, user histories, first-person video, or platform logs. A worker must decide what to fetch, what to ignore, when to ask another component, and when to stop. That makes the family a study of controlled action under uncertainty: the agent must map a vague human request onto a sequence of concrete, checkable steps without losing the user goal.
llm-agents-tool-use.naive_failure: A smart beginner would first give the model a big instruction: understand the request, pick any useful tool, and explain the final answer. That can work for small demonstrations, but the input papers repeatedly show why it breaks in real settings. Tool documentation may not use the same words as the user, so a tool selector retrieves the wrong API. Long conversations and biological sequences overflow the useful working memory, so important facts vanish. Multi-agent systems can add noise instead of clarity, as the feedback-generation paper reports when a well-designed single prompt often beats agent splitting. Production shopping agents must meet accuracy, latency, reliability, and cost limits at the same time. Security papers show a sharper failure: poisoned tool context or malicious knowledge-base documents can make the agent spend extra money or take unsafe actions. The simple plan fails because action creates consequences, not just text.
llm-agents-tool-use.mathematical_principle: The repeated mathematical idea is controlled search through a large menu of possible next moves. At each step, the agent has a goal, partial evidence, and many possible actions: rewrite the query, retrieve a tool, call a search system, consult memory, compress context, ask a specialist agent, roll back a suspicious state, or end the task. The math turns this into scoring and choice. Some papers train the chooser from reward: actions that lead to better tool use, stronger ranking, or fewer failed tasks receive more credit.
