Some arrange examples from easier to harder, so the model first learns clean choices before facing noisy and conflicting ones. Some route work by estimated difficulty, sending simple questions through cheaper paths and hard ones through deeper reasoning. Retrieval papers measure closeness between the user need and tool descriptions, documents, AppCards, schemas, or knowledge-graph facts. Security and evaluation papers measure deviation: does the current tool context, explanation, or user behavior look unlike a trusted path? The core tradeoff is exploration versus reliability, with cost, memory, and safety as hard operational limits in practice.
llm-agents-tool-use.why_math_matters: The math matters because the world has structure that a handwritten rule list cannot cover. User requests are varied, but many reduce to the same hidden question: which small set of outside resources should be trusted for this step? Tool repositories are huge, yet tools with related documentation, inputs, and past success patterns should be nearer to each other than unrelated tools. Dialogue histories are long, yet only some past facts matter for the present emotional-support reply. Mobile apps and web shopping flows differ, yet an agent can reuse the pattern of finding intent, gathering evidence, comparing options, and acting. Reward-based learning fits because success is often visible after the sequence: the workflow runs, the item ranking helps, the Android task succeeds, the policy simulation changes a predicted outcome, or the answer is grounded in retrieved evidence. The structure is not perfect, so the papers add filters, staged training, debate, rollback, routing, and explicit memory to keep the choice process from becoming blind confidence.
llm-agents-tool-use.paper_family: The tool-use papers are siblings because they all build gates between language and action. TOOL-CURE and Tool-Star focus on choosing and coordinating tools, using staged practice and feedback from success to reduce wrong calls. ToolBox-RL faces the same shape at repository scale: rewrite a user need, understand intent, and retrieve the right tool even when the words do not match the documentation. MCP servers for Pyserini and RankLLM expose search and ranking tools so an agent can ground answers in retrieval instead of guessing. The production shopping agent, Smart Book Seeker, and conversational search work apply the same gate to commerce and library discovery: turn a messy preference into retrieval, comparison, and action. PromptX, ES-MemEval, Frugal Agents, and the egocentric co-pilot treat memory and compressed context as tools that must be opened only when useful. CodeForge, COMA, GCAgent, and automated software-development agents split work across roles, but still face the same question: which voice or module should influence the next step? Security papers such as MCP remediation and cost attacks study what happens when the gate is deliberately misled before action.
llm-agents-tool-use.what_changed: The 2026 version shown here moves from impressive single-agent demos toward operating conditions. Many papers are about production limits, not just task scores: Amazon-scale shopping requires latency, cost, and reliability; EcoThink routes easy questions to save energy; TCR compresses heavier reasoning into a smaller ranker for real-time recommendation; Frugal Agents reduce long-context expense. The family also becomes more defensive. Tool poisoning, retrieval cost attacks, noisy user behavior, and biased code reasoning are treated as central problems. Finally, agents are becoming situated: they work over phone apps, web shopping, smart glasses video, group chats, therapy stages, historical-character data, and relational databases rather than only clean text prompts.
llm-agents-tool-use.limits: These papers assume that the agent can observe enough of the task to score its own progress or learn from past success. That may fail when the user goal is vague, private, changing, or only judged long after the action. Retrieval-based tool use assumes useful tools and documents can be found from descriptions; sparse metadata, poisoned entries, or missing evidence break that assumption. Multi-agent debate assumes separate roles add checks, but the feedback-generation result warns that splitting a task can lower consistency. Memory helps only if stored facts are true, current, and relevant. Simulations and benchmarks show controlled evidence, not proof that agents will behave safely under every deployment pressure, adversary, language, user literacy level, or cost constraint.

llms-language-models.problem_shape: These papers share one pressure: language models are no longer just chat boxes. They are being asked to read private training text without seeing it directly, judge whether content is safe for brands, explain clusters in changing graphs, translate low-resource languages, rank products, diagnose software traces, structure industrial requirements, and answer questions for different people in different moments. In each setting, the real object is messy human or operational information: logs, documents, personal histories, graphs, product records, languages, policies, and standards. The model must turn that mess into a useful action while staying faithful to the setting. The difficulty is that language is both flexible and slippery. The same words can mean different things by culture, time, user, task, or surrounding evidence. A model that sounds fluent may still expose private text, follow poisoned documents, invent preferences, miss graph structure, or carry hidden bias. This family is about making language models usable when fluency alone is not enough, especially when wrong answers affect systems, safety, markets, or people.
llms-language-models.naive_failure: A smart beginner might try to use a large language model as a universal reader: paste in the question, graph, log, item history, or policy, then trust the answer if it sounds coherent. That fails for several repeated reasons. Long inputs make the model pay attention to the wrong pieces. Sparse user histories leave gaps that it fills with plausible but false preferences. Web knowledge can be stale, poisoned, or culturally narrow. Private training signals can leak through updates even when raw data never leaves a device. Safety rules can be bypassed by changing the form of harmful content. Evaluation can also fool us: a model may agree with a query wording or a relevance threshold rather than the actual information need. The naive strategy treats language understanding as one skill, but the papers show many separate jobs: finding evidence, preserving structure, adapting to users, controlling cost, and checking trust.
llms-language-models.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is controlled transformation. Each paper asks: what information should be kept, changed, compared, hidden, or thrown away before the model speaks? In recommendation papers, user actions and item descriptions are turned into signs of preference, then candidates are sorted by how well they match later behavior or trend signals. In graph papers, nodes are people, items, or concepts, and links say that evidence should travel between neighbors; the model must keep that link structure instead of flattening everything into plain text. In security papers, small changes in model updates, compressed weights, retrieved documents, or prompt layout are measured to see whether they can reveal data or force bad behavior. In evaluation papers, answers are compared against clearer task descriptions, language coverage, or key evidence fragments. Some papers tune a model by changing a small set of settings and keeping the change only when it lowers a defined kind of error. Others compress a large model so it can run on a device, while trying not to lose the behavior needed for the task. The tradeoff is always compression versus trust: language models compress huge experience into reusable patterns, but every compression can erase context, leak information, or preserve the wrong signal.
llms-language-models.why_math_matters: The math matters because the world around these models has structure that ordinary prompting does not respect by itself. A microservice trace is not just words; it is a chain of events where timing and component identity matter. A recommendation history is not just a sentence about taste; it is an ordered record where later behavior can confirm or reject inferred preferences. An ontology proof is not persuasive because it sounds reasonable; each step must follow rules about which facts imply other facts. A multilingual safety test is not just translation; language and culture change what counts as bias or harm. Methods such as scoring candidates, spreading evidence through graphs, constraining decoding, selecting compact training examples, or merging model changes give the system handles on these structures. They let researchers state what should count as better: less leakage, better evidence use, lower cost, clearer relevance judgments, preserved non-target knowledge, or answers that fit a user's purpose. Without that stated target, the model's smooth wording can hide whether it used the right evidence, respected the right order, or merely repeated a familiar pattern from training.
llms-language-models.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they all add control around a fluent but unreliable language engine. The federated reconstruction work and LLMQuA both ask what hidden information can be recovered or changed from model-side traces, showing that privacy and safety depend on the mechanics of updates and compression. Jailbreak and retrieval-cost attacks make the same point from the outside: an attacker can change the form of text or poison the knowledge base so the model spends more, refuses wrongly, or answers unsafely. Conflict-aware retrieval, cost attacks on retrieval-augmented systems, SciCheck, and formalized information needs all treat outside evidence as something that must be selected, checked, and aligned with the final answer, not merely appended. Graph-tokenizing work, node role-guided clustering, semantic web workshops, and OWL proof evaluation make the same move for structure: they force the model to respect links, roles, and rules that prose alone can blur. SAGE, TM-Bench, Arabic relevance labeling, and long-tail web analysis expose the language coverage problem. Swen, NeurPIU, TRAIL, Rec2, and on-device recommendation turn the family toward users, where intent, memory, cost, and future behavior decide whether the model is useful.
llms-language-models.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that language models are being treated less as standalone answer machines and more as parts inside larger systems. The evidence shows more papers about deployment pressures: on-device recommendation, desktop assistance, industrial XML structuring, trace diagnosis, low-resource translation, and search agents. It also shows sharper concern about failure modes: privacy reconstruction, jailbreaks, poisoned retrieval, quantized-model backdoors, priming in relevance judgments, popularity bias from training exposure, and unbalanced forgetting. The center of gravity has moved from asking whether language models can do a task to asking what guardrails, evidence channels, user models, and tests make the result dependable.
llms-language-models.limits: These papers do not prove that language models are generally trustworthy. The evidence is mostly representative titles and short problem-method summaries, so the family view can identify shared pressures but cannot verify every claim or result. Many methods assume the chosen evidence source is relevant, the graph links mean something real, the user history reflects true preference, or the evaluation data covers the culture and language being tested. Security findings also cut both ways: an attack that works in one setup may not transfer, while a defense that blocks one form of harm may miss another. The family breaks when fluent text is mistaken for grounded reasoning, when hidden training exposure is treated as world knowledge, or when deployment cost and privacy constraints are ignored.

misinformation-trust.problem_shape: This family is about deciding what can be trusted when digital evidence is easy to copy, edit, generate, or present out of context. The real-world object may be a micro-video, a vaccine image, a sustainability claim, a scientific citation, a chatbot correction, a Community Note, an autonomous-driving simulation, a feedback label, or a security-camera stream. In every case, the system is not merely asking whether a piece of content looks plausible. It is asking where the claim came from, what evidence supports it, who checked it, whether private data can stay hidden, and whether the final confidence is deserved. The shared pressure is that trust now depends on a chain: source, content, context, retrieval, human judgment, model judgment, and sometimes cryptographic proof. A weak link can make a true-looking answer unsafe. These papers belong together because they treat misinformation and trust as evidence-management problems. They try to gather the right clues, compare them to reliable references, expose why a judgment was made, and prevent users or models from mistaking fluent presentation for verified truth.
misinformation-trust.naive_failure: A smart beginner would first build a classifier that labels content true or false, perhaps with a bigger language or vision model and a list of known bad examples. That fails because misinformation is not one stable visual or textual pattern. It can be a real image paired with the wrong event, a persuasive professional-looking fact-check, a video edited in small ways, a generated reference, a green claim that omits key context, or a crowd rating that changes after public display. Another simple idea is to retrieve evidence and trust whatever appears most similar. That fails when retrieved evidence is incomplete, irrelevant, manipulated, private, or too costly to check at scale. A third shortcut is to show a confidence score, but confidence can be overblown when the model has weak evidence. Across the family, the naive failure is treating trust as a single label rather than a chain of claims that must be inspected.
misinformation-trust.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is controlled comparison under uncertainty. Each paper starts by turning a messy trust question into smaller things that can be checked: a video frame against external evidence, a claim against a knowledge source, a citation against a repository, a user rating before and after display, a private feedback label against a proof rule, or a model answer against signals of internal stability. The math then asks which comparisons should count and how much confidence they deserve. Retrieval methods measure closeness between a claim and possible evidence, while accepting that closeness is only a clue, not proof. Ranking methods choose which evidence or explanation should be inspected first. Time-series methods compare behavior before and after an event, such as a Community Note being shown, to see whether public display changes agreement. Privacy and verification methods add carefully designed checks: a party can prove that a rule was followed or noise was added without revealing the underlying private data. The common tradeoff is evidence versus exposure: the system needs enough signal to judge trust, while hiding sensitive data, saving effort, and avoiding false certainty.
misinformation-trust.why_math_matters: The math matters because trust has structure that ordinary rules cannot handle. Evidence is often scattered across text, images, videos, graphs, databases, people, and time. A rule such as "look for suspicious words" misses out-of-context media, visual vaccine claims, fake scholarly references, and sustainability statements whose problem is omission rather than an obvious lie. A rule such as "trust the crowd" misses polarization and instability, as shown by work on Community Notes. A rule such as "trust the retrieved source" misses the fact that a generated answer can sound certain while the useful subgraph or repository match is incomplete. These papers use comparison, aggregation, calibration, proof, and sequence tracking because the world gives repeated partial clues, not perfect labels. Multimodal systems combine what is seen, said, and retrieved. Agent systems split the checking task across roles so weak clues do not drown out anomalies. Verification systems use public checks and hidden data together. The math is the language for balancing useful evidence, privacy, speed, and warranted confidence.
misinformation-trust.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they all repair a broken trust chain at different points. FakeAgent and TrueLens focus on video: they gather visual and outside evidence so a micro-video or fake-news clip is not judged by surface appearance alone. Concept-grounded vaccine detection and the out-of-context media paper handle mixed image-text claims by exposing visual, rhetorical, entity, and caption clues. EmeraldApp and CiteLLM move the same idea into claims about sustainability and scholarship, where the task is to ground a polished sentence in trusted sources rather than accept fluent wording. Chatbot correction and knowledge-graph answer calibration ask when an AI answer should be believed, especially across health, science, politics, or incomplete retrieved evidence. Community Notes, lateral browsing, rhetoric comparison, DREAMS, and misinformation forecasting study the human and social side: how people verify, persuade, rate, engage, and polarize over time. ZK-V, Trustless Feedback, Xemis, decentralized trust layers, video provenance, and agent governance form the infrastructure branch, where the answer is not better wording but verifiable records, privacy-preserving checks, and rules for who can prove what. The deeper move is shared: replace unsupported trust with inspectable evidence.
misinformation-trust.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is shaped by generated content and AI-mediated checking becoming ordinary web infrastructure. The evidence shows more work on videos, multimodal social posts, chatbot corrections, agentic systems, scholarly references, sustainability claims, and model confidence, not only text rumor detection. Trust is also moving from after-the-fact classification toward provenance, calibration, governance, and private verification. Several papers treat speed and deployment pressure as central: lightweight out-of-context detection, real-time recommendation trust, in-browser agent execution, edge video provenance, and low-overhead cryptographic receipts. Another change is that human trust is treated as dynamic. Community ratings, lateral browsing behavior, persuasion style, engagement sequences, and polarization signals all matter because the same claim can be accepted, rejected, or revived depending on context and timing.
misinformation-trust.limits: These papers depend on assumptions the input evidence cannot fully prove. Retrieved evidence must be relevant and not itself misleading. Concept features must capture the cues that actually matter, not just the cues that are easy to name. Crowd ratings and behavioral studies may change across platforms, topics, languages, and political climates. Cryptographic and decentralized systems can prove that a rule was followed, but they do not prove that the original rule, sensor, or human label was correct. Agent-based checkers can still inherit mistakes from their tools or retrieved sources. Confidence estimation helps only if its structural signals track real uncertainty. The evidence reports problems, approaches, and selected gains; it does not show long-term performance under coordinated manipulation, new media formats, legal pressure, or changing incentives.

multimodal-vision-language.problem_shape: This family is about systems that must understand a thing when the evidence arrives in different forms. A product has a title, image, price, and user behavior. A video has pictures, spoken words, comments, timing, and cultural cues. A robot or smart-glasses helper sees a scene, reads instructions, and must act. A medical image may show a small region whose meaning is described in language. The shared pressure is that no single channel is enough. Text can name a concept without showing where it appears. Images can show detail without saying what matters. Sensors can record motion without ordinary meaning. Graphs can show relationships without visual proof. The 204 papers in this theme, spread across WWW, SIGIR, WSDM, and KDD, are siblings because they all try to make these channels cooperate. The real task is not just recognizing pictures or parsing words. It is deciding which pieces of evidence from each channel should be compared, trusted, routed, explained, ranked, forgotten, or used for action.
multimodal-vision-language.naive_failure: A smart beginner would first process each channel separately: classify the image, read the text, score the user history, then combine the answers at the end. That fails because the hard cases live in the relation between channels. A hateful meme may hide meaning in the gap between image and caption. A web agent may read a button label but fail to locate the right screen element. A product campaign may use language that does not directly name the purchased product type. A sensor trace may describe an activity only after being tied to visual and textual context. The beginner might then force everything into one shared description and compare it directly. That also fails when channels are weakly aligned, culturally biased, missing, delayed, noisy, or too expensive to inspect fully. The problem is not mere mixing. It is deciding when two unlike signals are pointing to the same real thing.
multimodal-vision-language.mathematical_principle: The repeated mathematical idea is alignment: building a shared measuring space where unlike evidence can be compared without erasing what makes each channel different. In plain terms, the system learns that this image region, this phrase, this product type, this motion pattern, this graph relation, or this document screenshot may be different views of the same object or claim. Closeness means they support the same decision. Distance means they should not be treated as interchangeable. Some papers learn from paired or related examples, pulling matching views together and pushing misleading matches apart. Some distill knowledge, meaning they train a smaller model to copy useful reasoning from a larger image-and-language model so serving can be faster. Some route cases, sending only hard or uncertain examples to heavier visual reasoning. Others add structure: graph links, scene parts, bounding boxes, product relations, time windows, or explicit concepts. Ranking then orders candidates by how well the aligned evidence fits the current need. The tradeoff is compression versus detail: a shared comparison is useful only if it keeps the visual, textual, spatial, cultural, or temporal clue that the task actually depends on.
multimodal-vision-language.why_math_matters: The math matters because the world has repeated cross-channel structure, but it is not a dictionary. The word vaccine and a visual cue in a misinformation image may support the same stance, yet the system must show which cue mattered. A cover image and a buyer interest profile may fit even when the item has little click history. A traffic forecast may need satellite imagery, road layout, time, and event context because none of them alone explains congestion. A 3D scene query may ask for local structure that is not captured by a flat caption. Alignment methods exploit the fact that different channels often point to the same hidden situation. Scoring and routing matter because not every channel is worth equal cost in every case: StreamSense selectively escalates streaming signals, TCR compresses heavier reasoning for real-time recommendation, and cloud-end offloading decides where visual-language work should run. The mathematical rule gives these systems a repeatable way to balance accuracy, delay, cost, interpretability, and trust instead of hand-writing a special case for every media type.
multimodal-vision-language.paper_family: The representative papers are different branches of the same move: repair the bridge between channels before making the decision. PLIKD, structural adaptation for recommendation, HAAF, and fine-grained visual understanding ask how a large image-and-language model can adapt to new classes, products, or pathology details without overfitting the easy source cases. MCRec, RecCLIP-style collaborative filtering, campaign-to-product attribution, and multi-modal item relation learning use visual, textual, and behavior evidence to improve ranking when purchases or labels are sparse. StreamSense, task-aware offloading, TCR, and Vistar face the cost side of the same problem: use heavy cross-channel reasoning only where it changes the answer. Moderation and trust papers, including vaccine misinformation detection, hateful meme evaluation, moral-emotion analysis, claim verification, fact-checking, ToxiTwitch, and child-ad detection, treat alignment as evidence control: which visual or textual cue justifies a judgment, and does that cue transfer across cultures? PLM, WPIS, Struct-Align, geo-localization, Chain of Evidence, educational video evidence injection, web-interaction tuning, and the egocentric co-pilot extend the family into spatial action, asking not only what is present, but where it is, how it connects, and what a system should do next.
multimodal-vision-language.what_changed: The 2026 version shown here is less about proving that image and text can be joined, and more about making the joint reasoning usable under real pressure. The input papers emphasize cold-start recommendation, live streams, web automation, medical few-shot settings, low-resource dialect retrieval, cultural meme moderation, cloud and device cost, document screenshots, physical scene graphs, and adversarial attacks on vision-language-action models. They also ask for visible evidence: concepts, rationales, bounding boxes, provenance, graph structure, and state verification. The center has shifted from a general model that can describe media toward systems that must rank, moderate, navigate, verify, forget, retrieve, or act while showing why the cross-channel evidence should be trusted.
multimodal-vision-language.limits: These papers assume that channels can be aligned well enough for one to help another. That can fail when images and captions are sarcastic, culturally local, mistranslated, maliciously perturbed, or only loosely related. A shared measuring space can hide the exact visual detail that mattered, while explicit concepts can miss cues not named by the concept list. Distilled or routed systems save time only if the small model or router knows when it is uncertain. Cross-cultural and low-resource results depend on prompts, translations, and available paired data. Scene and navigation methods assume detected objects, spatial structure, and physical states are reliable. The input evidence reports approaches and claimed gains, not proof that these systems remain trustworthy across every platform, culture, adversary, device, or deployment setting.

privacy-federated-security.problem_shape: This family is about systems that need help from data they are not allowed to freely collect, expose, or trust. Hospitals, phones, recommender services, browsers, sensor networks, blockchains, metro systems, and web domains all hold useful signals, but those signals can reveal people, business secrets, security weaknesses, or private training text. The shared real-world task is therefore not simply to learn a better model or audit a safer web service. It is to move useful evidence across organizational or device boundaries while keeping the dangerous parts hidden, and while assuming that some participants or attackers may lie, steal, poison, or infer what was meant to stay private. The 168 papers in this family circle the same pressure from different sides. Federated work keeps raw data local but must still combine learning. Privacy work adds noise, proofs, or partial sharing so outsiders cannot read sensitive details. Security work asks where sharing itself opens a door: stolen cookies, leaked model behavior, poisoned tools, attacked blockchains, exposed WebAssembly models, or side channels. The family exists because modern web intelligence is collaborative, but collaboration turns privacy and security from add-on features into the core engineering problem.
privacy-federated-security.naive_failure: A smart beginner would keep private data on each device or organization, send only model updates or summary patterns to a shared server, and add a simple access rule saying who may participate. That is a reasonable first move because it avoids the most obvious leak: copying raw records into one database. It fails because summaries can still reveal details. The adapter-based federated language model attack shows that training updates can be worked backward into training text. Membership inference work shows that a model can betray whether a changed sentence was in its web training data. A second beginner move is to hide more information by adding noise, but too much noise makes the learned system less useful and unfairly weakens careful contributors. A third move is to trust participants, domains, tools, or validators once authenticated. The evidence shows why that breaks: clients can poison shared graph learning, subdomains can leak cookies, agents can be tricked by poisoned tools, and blockchain validators can collude.
privacy-federated-security.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is constrained sharing: decide exactly what useful signal may cross a boundary, what sensitive detail must be blocked, and how to check that the boundary was respected. In federated learning, the local holder keeps records and sends a shaped update, prototype, small adapter, or other summary. The central question is what that summary preserves. It should carry enough pattern to improve recommendations, graph clustering, fault diagnosis, metro forecasting, signal recovery, or multimodal learning, but not enough to reconstruct a person, sentence, sensor trace, or business dataset. Differential privacy is the noise version of this idea: deliberately blur each contribution so one record has limited visible effect, while preserving repeated patterns that appear across many records. Zero-knowledge proof systems are the verification version: prove that a rule was followed without revealing the private circuit, telemetry, identity credential, or simulation trace itself. Poisoning defenses and anomaly detectors are the trust version: compare incoming behavior against expected density, timing, memory, or update patterns and flag signals that look too strategically shaped. Incentive and blockchain papers add a payment and reputation layer, asking how to reward real contribution and punish free-riding. The tradeoff is useful cooperation versus leakage, verification versus cost, and privacy versus accuracy.
privacy-federated-security.why_math_matters: The math matters because privacy and security failures are rarely visible in the raw surface of a system. A training update, browser module, cookie rule, blockchain action, or graph prototype may look harmless while carrying hidden information or hidden attack intent. The family needs measured constraints because hand-written promises such as share less, trust the server, or encrypt the channel do not answer the harder question: how much can an observer still infer after seeing the allowed output? Noise budgets matter because privacy is not all-or-nothing; every shared result spends some exposure, and DIARY treats recovery after unlearning as another place where exposure can be spent badly. Prototype alignment matters because clients may have different cluster counts or personal behavior patterns, so a single average can erase local structure. Density checks matter because poisoned graph updates may sit in strange regions compared with normal shared patterns. Formal proof systems matter because Blind-QEM, ZK-V, and USIM-less authentication need verifiable compliance without revealing the thing being checked. Security measurement also needs counting and comparison at scale: CookieDrift and Internet security indicators turn scattered weaknesses into measured exposure across domains. These tools exploit repeated structure while limiting what any single private case can reveal.
privacy-federated-security.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each asks what can safely cross a boundary. Reconstructing Training Data from Adapter-based Federated Large Language Models and Decoding Web Memorization study the leak side: even when only updates or model behavior are visible, an attacker may infer hidden training text or membership. FeedGuard, RAFed, FedUMM, FedRMamba, federated signal recovery, and MF3 study the utility side: phones, sensors, transit systems, and multimodal clients need joint learning without centralizing records, so they pass selected updates, small adapters, or pattern summaries. FedCND, pFedDKS, Thorki, PAECL, prototype-aligned soft prompts, and verifiable federated recommendation show personalization pressure: clients are not copies of one another, so the system must separate shared structure from local needs. Poisoning and backdoor papers, including federated knowledge graph attacks and fairness-aware federated finance, treat collaboration as an attack surface where bad participants can bend the shared model. Xemis, WinFLoRA, DIARY, and the blockchain incentive paper focus on governance: noise, reward, rollback, and contribution scoring decide whether cooperation remains fair. Blind-QEM, ZK-V, USIM-less authentication, quantum-safe blockchain tutorials, and ZABAPAD move the same logic into cryptographic verification. Cookie theft, doxing, WebAssembly isolation, browser model obfuscation, selfish mining, tool poisoning, and RAG cost attacks widen the family beyond federated learning into web systems where hidden channels and strategic behavior turn sharing into risk.
privacy-federated-security.what_changed: The 2026 version is broader and more adversarial than a simple private-training story. The evidence is dominated by WWW papers but also includes SIGIR, WSDM, and KDD, showing that privacy and security now touch search, recommendation, graph learning, language models, blockchains, browsers, and infrastructure measurement. The newer emphasis is on leakage after apparent protection: adapter updates leak text, semantic changes still reveal membership, recovery after unlearning creates another privacy phase, and outsourced quantum or driving verification must prove compliance without exposing the private object. Federated work is also becoming more personalized and heterogeneous. Papers handle different client data shapes, privacy choices, model sizes, cluster counts, modalities, and incentives instead of assuming one uniform client population.
privacy-federated-security.limits: These papers assume the shared summaries, noise rules, proofs, measurements, or anomaly scores capture the real risk. That can fail when attackers adapt, when normal clients are highly unusual, or when side channels expose information outside the modeled boundary. Federated learning assumes local data holders are numerous or diverse enough that shared patterns are useful; sparse clients, extreme non-uniform data, or low-quality participants can weaken both accuracy and privacy. Noise-based protection assumes the privacy budget is calibrated to the setting, but the input evidence does not prove one setting transfers to another. Verification papers can prove a narrow rule while leaving surrounding software, incentives, or deployment choices vulnerable. Security measurement papers reveal exposure in studied domains or traces, not the full web.

recommender-systems.problem_shape: These papers share one pressure: a system must choose a small set of useful things from a huge, changing pile. The thing may be a product, video, search result, explanation, dialogue response, image-rich item, or even a fine-grained urban indicator inferred from user-business activity. The system rarely sees the whole person or the whole item. It sees clicks, purchases, text, images, graph links, conversations, timestamps, and noisy controls such as dislike buttons. From that partial evidence it must decide what to show next, what to explain, and what not to over-show. The hard part is that usefulness is not one number. Accuracy can fight discovery, popularity can hide niche items, engagement can fight trust, and short-term clicks can create long-term traps. The 452-paper venue spread in this family shows how central this pressure is across WWW, SIGIR, WSDM, and KDD. The papers are siblings because they all try to make selection more faithful when user intent, item meaning, time, fairness, cost, and feedback loops are all moving at once.
recommender-systems.naive_failure: A smart beginner would start by counting what people clicked, bought, watched, or rated, then show similar people the same popular items. That works when users are stable, items are simple, and the goal is only immediate response. It fails in the settings represented here. New users have little history, long histories are expensive to read, and old behavior can drown out recent change. Popular items get repeated because they already have evidence, while rare or niche items stay unseen. Text, images, and graph links can disagree, and some items are missing one of those signals. A single model can also treat every case with the same effort, even though some candidates are easy to reject and others require careful comparison. Worse, feedback from the recommender changes the future data, so the system may learn from patterns it helped create.
recommender-systems.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is to turn recommendation into controlled comparison under uncertainty. The system gives users, items, moments, explanations, and objectives compact descriptions, then asks which candidates are closest to the current need and which order best serves the chosen goal. Closeness may come from shared behavior, item text, images, graph neighbors, dialogue history, or sequence position. Ranking then turns many scores into a short ordered list, while losses define what counts as a bad order and training repeatedly reduces that badness. Several papers change the comparison itself: Talos replaces expensive full ranking with sampled score-threshold comparisons; graph methods let evidence travel along user-item or line-graph links; multimodal papers align visual, textual, and relational signals so they can be compared; cold-start papers use semantic search, generated preference descriptions, or selected examples when click history is scarce. Other papers add constraints: fairness methods limit popularity bias, multi-objective methods balance competing goals, calibration checks whether recommendation proportions match changing user tastes, and efficiency methods compress long sequences or use sparse comparisons so time, memory, serving delay, and user patience do not explode.
recommender-systems.why_math_matters: The math matters because the world has reusable structure but not perfect labels. People with related histories often give useful clues about one another, but only if the system notices which parts of the history are relevant now. Items with similar text, images, or graph positions often answer similar needs, but auxiliary visual objects, missing modalities, and noisy dialogue can point the system in the wrong direction. Time has structure too: a recent purchase may matter more than an old browsing path, yet papers such as Retracing and Restoring argue that old context should not simply be overwritten. Optimization, meaning choosing settings by reducing a defined error, gives these systems a way to trade off accuracy, cost, fairness, freshness, and diversity instead of hard-coding rules for every case. Probability-based search and multi-objective methods help when the system is unsure which goal a user values. Graph and sequence methods help when the useful signal is not in one event, but in how events, people, and items connect.
recommender-systems.paper_family: The representative papers form branches of the same deeper move: repair the comparison before making the recommendation. RobustExplain and Auditing Textual Context ask whether explanations remain useful when behavior or text is noisy. Talos, heterogeneity-aware pre-ranking, HyenaRec, sparse long-behavior modeling, and categorical sequence compression focus on making the short-listing step cheaper without losing the candidates that matter. FairLRM, FUDLR, neuron steering, FairFS, and post-training fairness control treat recommendation as a ranked choice that can unfairly amplify popular items or biased features unless the system can inspect and adjust its signals. TargetMR, Triple Modality Fusion, and missing-modality early fusion address the same issue for item meaning: text, image, and graph evidence must be aligned before scores are trusted. RAIE, continual learning, calibration, and chronological restoration handle moving preferences. GALRec, line graphs, graph-based urban inference, and hypergraph simulations show how link structure can carry evidence or create cocoons. Conversational and cold-start papers, including EyeCRS, MOCHA, MARS, and causal diffusion preference modeling, ask how to recommend when history is sparse, hidden, new, ambiguous, incomplete, contested, private, or partly harmful to the next decision.
recommender-systems.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is less about whether recommenders can predict clicks and more about whether they can be steered, explained, updated, and afforded in real settings. Large language models appear often, but mainly as tools that create new pressures: they can explain, generate, route among models, and use item language, yet they also import bias, forget updated preferences, ignore graph signals, or use irrelevant dialogue history. The family also shifts toward deployment concerns: Walmart multimodal ranking, Kuaishou e-commerce ranking, YouTube control audits, federated device differences, long behavior sequences, missing modalities, and fairness changes after training. The central change is recommendation under operational pressure, not recommendation as a clean offline sorting task.
recommender-systems.limits: These papers assume that the recorded signals are meaningful enough to guide future choices. That can fail when clicks reflect habit, manipulation, limited exposure, or the recommender's own past decisions rather than real preference. Graph links can spread useful evidence, but they can also spread popularity bias or social cocoon effects. Text and images can reveal item meaning, but they may miss why a person wants something now. Fairness and human-centered metrics depend on which stakeholders and values are measured. Efficiency papers show cheaper comparison, but cost savings do not prove better long-term user welfare. The input evidence reports problems, approaches, and selected contributions, not full proofs that these methods work across all platforms, cultures, item types, or changing business goals.

reinforcement-learning.problem_shape: These papers share a decision problem: a web system must act now, observe what happened, and use that feedback to act better next time. The action may be entering a marketplace, choosing a seller policy, crawling a changing graph, spending an ad budget, rewriting a query, selecting a tool, tuning a blockchain, defending a fraud detector, or steering an agent through a conversation. The common pressure is not just prediction. A prediction says what might happen; these papers need a choice that changes what happens next. That makes the evidence circular. A recommender creates the clicks it later learns from. A crawler changes which pages are seen. A bidding system spends money that cannot be recovered. A privacy system gains useful feedback only by risking exposure. A security paper may train an attacker and defender inside the same loop. The family belongs together because 110 papers treat learning as repeated trial, score, adjustment, and constraint, spread heavily across WWW and SIGIR with smaller groups in WSDM and KDD.
reinforcement-learning.naive_failure: A smart beginner would write rules: spend more where returns looked high yesterday, crawl pages that changed recently, pick the tool whose documentation matches the query, recommend items close to past clicks, or block attacks that match known patterns. Those rules fail because the best action is often hidden until after trying something. Acting only on yesterday's winner can miss new sellers, new attacks, new user needs, or better long-term strategies. Acting too broadly wastes money, time, privacy, and attention. The system also faces delayed credit: a good clarification question, query rewrite, seed choice, or ad bid may matter several steps later, while a bad early choice may poison the later evidence. In these papers, the simple rule fails because it treats each decision as isolated, even though the outcome depends on the sequence of earlier choices.
reinforcement-learning.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is learning a policy, meaning a rule for choosing the next action from the current situation, by judging the rewards and costs that follow. In plain language, the system tries an action, receives a score, and slowly changes its future choices toward actions that led to better scores under similar conditions. The score may be profit, search relevance, saved latency, lower privacy leakage, better calibration, stakeholder satisfaction, successful tool use, safer fraud detection, or a more useful retrieved document. Some papers add exploration, which means deliberately trying uncertain actions because always taking the known best option can trap the system in a narrow habit. Others add constraints, which are boundaries the learner should not cross, such as budget limits, privacy guarantees, fairness needs, millisecond latency, or risk of ruin. Game models add another layer: the learner's action changes how sellers, users, attackers, or defenders respond. The learner is therefore not just fitting past examples. It is estimating which choice will make the next few steps better. The tradeoff is short-term reward versus long-term learning, speed versus careful search, personalization versus privacy, and flexible adaptation versus dependable safety.
reinforcement-learning.why_math_matters: The math matters because these systems have a structure that ordinary scoring misses: present choices shape future evidence. A marketplace entry choice changes seller exploration incentives. A crawler's next visit decides which parts of an evolving graph become visible. A recommendation agent's question or item affects what the user reveals afterward. A budget allocator's early spending changes later money, risk, and reinvestment. A retrieval attack poisons a knowledge base so a language model later retrieves costly material. This is why repeated decision math fits the family. It gives each paper a way to connect an action, the state of the world before the action, the feedback after the action, and the next state. Probability enters because the same action can have different outcomes, so the system estimates chances from repeated cases rather than trusting one example. Control enters because actions must be adjusted while the process is still running. The useful structure is sequence: feedback is not a label attached to one record, but a trail left by choices over time.
reinforcement-learning.paper_family: The representative papers are different versions of one deeper move: close the loop between action and feedback. FeedGuard uses privacy-protected recommendation feedback so online adaptation can happen without exposing raw user data. ToolBox-RL, TOOL-CURE, REFLEX, PicQue, Triple-R, ReSuMe, and Deep GraphRAG all apply the same loop to search and tool use: rewrite, retrieve, rerank, or summarize, then use downstream usefulness as the teaching signal. Marketing Hosting, DARA, GAM, AHBid, and DeFi arbitrage treat money as a scarce resource whose use must be learned over time under constraints, not assigned once at the start. Dynamic graph crawling, DynaFLUX, and hypergraph distillation use feedback to decide where evidence should travel or which parts of a structure deserve attention. Security papers invert the same logic: inference-cost attacks, backdoor attacks, SoftHist, ransomware unlearning, and privacy-risk games ask how attackers or defenders improve after observing system response. The platform-entry paper adds strategic sellers, where one actor's learned policy changes another actor's incentive to explore. Agent and language-model papers, including GIMO, Prism, Intelli-Planner, RL with verbalized probabilities, and web-agent entropy balancing, use feedback to train multi-step behavior rather than one-shot answers.
reinforcement-learning.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family seems less centered on game-playing style reinforcement learning and more on deployed web loops. The evidence shows recommendation, retrieval, advertising, graph crawling, blockchain tuning, finance, privacy, ransomware detection, fact-checking, translation, hate detection, urban planning, and tool-using agents. Large language models are common, but mainly as systems that need feedback-guided behavior: they rewrite queries, choose tools, clarify intent, estimate probabilities, reason over evidence, or act as stakeholders in simulations. Another change is constraint pressure. Papers repeatedly mention privacy, budgets, latency, sparse feedback, long-tail content, data deletion, fairness, risk of ruin, and adversarial response. The learner is no longer just chasing a reward; it must learn while staying within operational boundaries.
reinforcement-learning.limits: These papers assume the feedback signal is trustworthy enough to teach from. That can fail when clicks reflect platform exposure, when user rewards are sparse or delayed, when attackers adapt faster than defenders, or when a simulator does not match real people. A learned policy can optimize the measured score while missing unmeasured harm, such as addiction, privacy leakage, unfair exposure, or long-term seller behavior. Constraints are only as good as their definitions: formal privacy, budget safety, or fairness guarantees may not cover every practical risk. Exploration can discover better choices, but it can also waste money or expose users to poor actions. The input evidence reports problems, approaches, and contributions, not full proof that these loops hold across every platform, culture, market, workload, or adversarial setting.

retrieval-augmented-rag.problem_shape: This family is about answer systems that should not rely only on what a language model already carries inside itself. The real task is to answer, forecast, teach, diagnose, recommend, or detect danger by first going out to a collection of outside evidence: web pages, documents, graph neighborhoods, medical knowledge, city histories, threat reports, or user interaction records. The shared problem is that outside evidence is both necessary and dangerous. Without it, the system may invent facts, miss recent changes, or ignore local knowledge. With it, the system may pull in stale, irrelevant, low-quality, conflicting, poisoned, or needlessly expensive material. A retrieval-augmented system therefore has two jobs that cannot be separated: it must choose evidence from a large pile, then use that evidence without being misled by it. The 182 papers in this family sit at that boundary between search and generation. They ask what should be fetched, how much should be fetched, when to fetch again, how to judge document quality, how to follow linked evidence, and when the final answer should admit uncertainty.
retrieval-augmented-rag.naive_failure: A smart beginner would connect a search engine to a language model: take the user question, fetch the top documents, paste them into the prompt, and let the model answer. This is sensible because many errors come from missing outside facts. It fails because the top documents are not all equally useful. Some may repeat each other, answer the wrong part of a multi-step question, disagree with each other, or contain planted text meant to waste computation or push a false answer. More retrieval is not a cure, because long evidence lists can bury the key fact, increase cost, and make the model forget earlier support during a reasoning chain. Static retrieval also fails when the world changes, when the task is predictive rather than factual, when the evidence is a graph or an image-text pair, or when medical and security settings require explicit verification rather than plausible wording.
retrieval-augmented-rag.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is evidence selection under uncertainty. In everyday terms, each possible piece of outside information gets treated as a candidate witness. The system asks several questions before trusting it: is it close to the current need, does it cover a missing part of the question, does it agree or conflict with other witnesses, does its source look useful, and is the cost of reading it worth the likely gain? Ranking turns these judgments into an order, where earlier evidence has more influence on the answer. Uncertainty estimates ask how shaky the system is before or during generation, so retrieval can happen only when the current answer lacks support. Graph methods treat facts, chunks, entities, or events as linked objects; a link says that neighboring evidence may explain or verify the current point. Calibration means making confidence match the strength of the retrieved support instead of the smoothness of the final text. Security papers add adversarial scoring: a document is not only relevant or irrelevant, but possibly harmful because it can raise cost, poison a graph path, or corrupt image-text fusion. The tradeoff is completeness versus distraction, trust versus speed, and stronger grounding versus greater attack surface.
retrieval-augmented-rag.why_math_matters: The math matters because useful evidence has structure. A question is often not one need but a chain of smaller needs. PruneRAG uses that shape by decomposing a question and expanding retrieval only where confidence is low, saving work while trying to preserve support. Evidence-chain work treats reasoning as a path where each step should have visible backing, because a fact that is merely nearby may not help the final inference. Graph retrieval exploits linked structure: in DA-RAG, relevant chunks can be found by searching a community around the query rather than treating every passage as isolated; in knowledge-graph systems, missing or unreliable subgraphs can make a model too confident unless uncertainty is recalibrated. Document-quality work matters because retrieved passages differ in relevance, ranking position, and predicted usefulness, so generation should not treat them as equal. Conflict-aware methods matter because two plausible sources can point in opposite directions, and the answer system needs a way to notice disagreement before merging them. These measured comparisons are needed because a hand-written rule cannot consistently balance relevance, diversity, conflict, cost, and safety across changing corpora and tasks.
retrieval-augmented-rag.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because each changes where trust is earned in a retrieval-augmented answer. Conflict-Aware RAG and Active Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Conflict-Fused Uncertainty Quantification put conflict near the center: they look for disagreement and uncertainty before deciding what to retrieve or prefer. OpenDecoder and SeaRAG focus on evidence quality at generation time, asking the model to weigh document quality, statements, entities, and uncertainty rather than simply consuming whatever was fetched. PruneRAG and NeocorRAG both treat multi-step reasoning as a managed evidence process: one prunes a query tree to reduce unnecessary retrieval, while the other mines evidence chains and measures whether retrieved material actually converts into better recall. DA-RAG and the causality-aware knowledge graph work use linked evidence, but with different worries: one searches dynamic attributed communities, while the other asks when an incomplete graph should lower confidence. IRAG, KEPo, and inference-cost attacks show the hostile side of the same design: attackers can poison documents, graph evolution paths, or multimodal evidence so retrieval makes the model worse or more expensive. Rise, xRAG4TS, IntelGuard, predictive RAG, and MGK-RAG show the family spreading into education, city forecasting, malicious package detection, recommendation, and radiology, where outside knowledge must fit the domain structure.
retrieval-augmented-rag.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is less about adding retrieved text and more about governing evidence. The input shows work across WWW, SIGIR, WSDM, and KDD, with a heavy concentration in SIGIR and WWW, which fits a field joining search practice with answer generation. The newer concerns are conflict, confidence, document quality, graph structure, attack resistance, and cost. Retrieval is becoming adaptive: systems decide when to retrieve, which branch of a question to expand, which source deserves more weight, and which evidence should be ignored. The setting is also broader than factual question answering, reaching education, forecasting, medical report generation, software supply-chain security, image-text evidence, and personalized prediction.
retrieval-augmented-rag.limits: These papers assume that useful evidence exists in the connected collection and that the system can recognize enough of it. That can fail when the corpus is stale, sparse, poisoned, badly chunked, or missing the domain facts needed for the question. Conflict detection assumes disagreement is visible in the retrieved material; hidden omissions can still look confident. Graph methods assume links mean real support, but forged or noisy links can spread false evidence. Confidence-guided retrieval can stop too early when the model is wrongly sure. Medical, education, security, and forecasting uses also require domain checks beyond fluent answers. The input evidence reports representative problems and contributions, but it does not prove that the methods generalize across deployments, attackers, languages, or changing knowledge bases.

self-supervised-contrastive.problem_shape: This family is about learning useful structure when the system has too few trusted labels, or when labels would be too slow, expensive, narrow, or stale to collect. The shared real-world problem is not one task. It appears when grouping graphs, finding social events, detecting audio deepfakes, matching sensor motion to text, checking facts, spotting anomalous subgraphs, retrieving documents, recommending items, aligning entities, and finding new graph classes. In each case, the system sees many raw objects but lacks a clear answer key for what each object means. The papers therefore ask the data to create its own teaching signal. Two graph views, two media views, a clean and changed passage, a current and remembered retrieval state, or a high-confidence and low-confidence group become evidence about what should stay together and what should be kept apart. The family pressure is scale and ambiguity: web, graph, language, sensor, image, and shopping data change faster than people can label them. The central task is to turn unlabeled traces into reliable comparisons without letting noise teach the wrong lesson.
self-supervised-contrastive.naive_failure: A smart beginner would first collect labels for every class, event, item relation, graph type, or fake-news case, then train a model to copy those labels. That fails when the event set is unknown, as in open-world social event detection, or when the graph contains mixed normal and anomalous examples without a clean training split. The beginner might then use simple similarity: group items that share words, neighbors, visual cues, or user behavior. That also fails because the same surface clue can mean different things. Popular products can drown out niche interests, sparse item behavior can hide substitute and complementary relations, short texts can produce noisy group names, and changed passages can preserve meaning while fooling retrieval or privacy checks. The next fallback is to trust the model's own guesses, but repeated self-training can amplify early mistakes. The problem is not just missing labels; it is missing labels while the available clues are uneven, noisy, and sometimes misleading.
self-supervised-contrastive.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is comparison-based learning from constructed evidence. Instead of waiting for a human answer key, the system builds pairs or groups that should agree in some important way, then learns settings that pull those agreeing cases closer and push competing cases farther away. Closeness here means a compressed description of an object: a graph neighborhood, document meaning, sensor motion, item image, user session, audio segment, entity profile, or taxonomy position. The compression is useful only if it preserves the relation the task needs. Some papers create multiple views of the same object, such as structure and semantics in graph clustering, collaborative and media views in recommendation, or motion, vision, and text in Vistar. Some create altered examples to test what should matter, such as counterfactual passages in retrieval or semantically changed samples for membership inference. Others add confidence, clustering, memory, uncertainty, or frequency splitting so bad self-made examples do not dominate. The system is always choosing which comparisons should count strongly, weakly, or not at all. The tradeoff is compression versus detail, useful agreement versus false agreement, and adaptation versus reinforcing a mistaken guess.
self-supervised-contrastive.why_math_matters: The math matters because these datasets contain repeated structure that is real but not directly named. Nearby graph nodes often share evidence, but links can also reflect popularity or noise. Two media sources can describe the same event, product, activity, or medical region, but their raw signals look nothing alike. User sessions reveal intention, but the final clicked item can confuse different journeys that happen to end in the same place. A document passage may be irrelevant in most words yet decisive in one sentence. These papers need scoring rules because the system must decide which similarities deserve trust. Confidence scoring, clustering, resampling, memory, uncertainty estimates, and multi-view alignment are ways to ration trust across imperfect signals. Frequency-based methods separate broad common patterns from local or niche patterns, so popularity does not erase minority interests. Hierarchical methods preserve coarse and fine structure at once. The repeated world structure is that meaning often survives changes in surface form, while noise often travels through the same channels. Mathematical comparison gives the system a way to keep one and dampen the other.
self-supervised-contrastive.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they all turn unlabeled or weakly labeled data into controlled comparisons. Hierarchical Graph-Bag-Network and Graph-to-Tree both say that a graph should not be treated as one flat object; useful evidence lives at several sizes, from local pieces to larger roles. Structure-Semantic Synergized Deep Contrastive Graph Clustering and UTAG add a second tension: graph links and text meaning must agree without one erasing the other. LFEvent, Vistar, multi-view recommendation, and item-relation learning use the same family logic across media, asking whether text, images, sensor motion, behavior, or language-model help point to the same underlying event, activity, or product relation. HierCon and the histopathology work apply comparison to detection, where the system must separate subtle fake or disease signals from ordinary similarity. CREAM, adaptive expert aggregation, and open-world graph active learning focus on change: old groupings must adapt when topics, class sets, or tabular regions move. Counterfactual retrieval, web memorization attacks, fact checking, and fake-news detection show a more adversarial branch, where the comparison must notice what information is decisive, noisy, copied, or deceptive. The surface tasks differ, but the mechanical question is shared: what should be treated as the same kind of thing?
self-supervised-contrastive.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family is broader and more deployment-shaped. Self-made supervision is no longer used only to pretrain a general model; it is being placed inside retrieval systems, recommenders, fact checkers, graph tools, medical segmentation, sensor interpretation, peer-review auditing, delivery-time prediction, and blockchain analysis. The papers also show more concern with bad self-teaching. Many add confidence filters, uncertainty estimates, selective sampling, clustering repair, memory, or external semantic guidance because noisy generated labels can cause durable errors. Another change is cross-modal and cross-domain pressure: language models, graph models, images, motion sensors, product behavior, and knowledge graphs are being aligned so one source can help another when direct labels are absent.
self-supervised-contrastive.limits: The family depends on the constructed comparisons being more right than wrong. If two views do not truly describe the same object, if graph neighbors are biased, if popular behavior overwhelms niche evidence, or if a language model supplies misleading semantic help, the method can confidently learn the wrong structure. Self-training and pseudo-labeling assume early guesses are good enough to refine; the NER and clustering papers explicitly face the risk that mistakes compound. Cross-domain and streaming methods assume old signals still contain transferable structure after the data changes. Detection and privacy-attack papers assume altered examples reveal the decisive difference rather than accidental artifacts. The input evidence reports many improvements, but it does not prove that these systems remain reliable under new users, adversaries, institutions, languages, sensors, or labeling standards.

social-networks-influence.problem_shape: This family is about people, accounts, places, posts, comments, payments, roads, and events that do not act alone. Each item is partly explained by the items around it: a friend-of-a-friend may become a recommendation, a comment may change a privacy choice, a harmful reply may shift a mental-health trajectory, and a rumor, emotion, or opinion may move through a crowd. The shared problem is that the useful signal is not stored in one record. It sits in the pattern of links, timing, groups, and feedback. That is why these papers keep returning to social networks, traffic networks, temporal graphs, signed networks, information cocoons, and platform interventions. They are trying to answer questions such as who influences whom, which groups are forming, which users or nodes matter, what will happen next, and whether a decision treats groups fairly. The hard part is that links can mean friendship, disagreement, exposure, shared context, money flow, location proximity, or manipulation. A link is evidence, but it is never automatically truth.
social-networks-influence.naive_failure: A smart beginner might start by counting simple facts: how many neighbors a user has, how often two accounts interact, which words appear in posts, which comments are positive, or which node sits near many others. That works when links are clean and when similar people connect to similar people. Many papers here show why that assumption breaks. Some networks connect opposites, not lookalikes. Some graphs are sparse, incomplete, directed, or missing because of privacy limits. Some influence appears only over time, as with opinion rhythm, event waves, next behavior, or mental-state change after comments. Group fairness also breaks simple counting, because a high-scoring pattern can still over-serve one group or expose sensitive attributes. In short, the first idea treats the network as a flat map, while the real setting is a moving social system with hidden motives, uneven data, and feedback loops.
social-networks-influence.mathematical_principle: The central mathematical move is to treat a social setting as a set of objects connected by paths, layers, times, and constraints, then ask how evidence should travel through those connections. A node might be a person, post, road region, wallet, event, or account. A link might mean friendship, reply, location closeness, transaction, shared sentiment, or possible influence. The math asks which neighbors should be trusted, how far evidence should move, whether a pattern repeats over time, and what must be balanced while making a decision. Some papers measure local shape, such as four-cycles, sparse graph structure, signed communities, or node removal. Others estimate spread, such as opinion propagation, information cocoons, peer comments, social conformity, or influence without visible topology. Others add constraints: group representation in streaming clustering, fairness-aware graph encoding, fair opinion distribution, and fair graph unlearning. The plain idea is not just that connected things are similar. It is that relationships create pressure, but different relationships carry different kinds of pressure. The tradeoff is local evidence versus global consistency, prediction accuracy versus fairness, and useful influence modeling versus privacy and missing links.
social-networks-influence.why_math_matters: The math matters because these problems are too tangled for hand-written rules. A rule like "trust close neighbors" fails when neighbors disagree, when bots deliberately look unlike their surroundings, or when harmful and supportive comments push mental state in opposite directions. A rule like "pick the biggest spreaders" fails when the visible network is hidden, noisy, or protected. A rule like "serve the best cluster centers" can fail group representation. Graph structure gives a way to keep many small relations at once instead of reducing everything to one table row. Time-aware models give a way to separate a lasting pattern from a short burst. Sampling and streaming methods give a way to inspect massive networks without storing every edge forever. Fairness constraints state what the system is not allowed to sacrifice while it searches for a useful answer. The recurring structure in the world is interdependence: one person's state, choice, or label is partly shaped by neighbors, events, and earlier signals. These papers need math because the question is usually not whether one link exists, but how much that link should matter among thousands or millions of competing links.
social-networks-influence.paper_family: Several branches in the evidence are versions of the same deeper move: decide how social evidence should move, and where it should stop. Graph Aggregation Beyond Homophily and IVQ-GNN both challenge the simple belief that connected nodes should look alike; they try to handle networks where unlike nodes are meaningful. SNBot uses the gap between an account and its neighborhood as a clue for bot detection rather than smoothing that gap away. Opinion and influence papers make the same issue dynamic. Rhythm of Opinion models how sentiment can echo over time, Fairness in Opinion-Formation Dynamics asks whether influence is fairly distributed across groups, and DynaFLUX tries to choose spreaders even when the visible topology is missing. The privacy and fairness papers add guardrails: FairGE avoids reconstructing sensitive attributes, FairGU studies what happens when graph unlearning changes fairness, and fair k-center clustering tries to keep group representation while processing streams. Other papers widen the evidence: multiplex community detection adds grievance and moral layers, Unicoon and PolicySim simulate platform feedback, and suicide-risk or depression-screening work treats comments and posts as time-varying social evidence rather than isolated text.
social-networks-influence.what_changed: The 2026 shape of this family is less about proving that networks matter and more about making network reasoning survive messy deployment conditions. The evidence repeatedly mentions massive streams, incomplete graphs, sparse social networks, hidden topology, temporal behavior, multimodal inputs, and fairness under sensitive or missing attributes. The papers also move from static description toward intervention: selecting fair centers, adjusting stubbornness in opinion dynamics, choosing spreaders without visible links, dismantling networks, simulating policy before deployment, or checking whether peer comments backfire. Another shift is evaluation pressure. Workshops and benchmark-style papers in the input emphasize trustworthiness, ethics, reproducibility, and bias across cultures, suggesting that social-network work is being judged not only by prediction but by whether its assumptions and side effects are visible.
social-networks-influence.limits: These explanations depend on the input metadata, not full papers or verified experiments. The abstracts and summaries say what each work claims to do, but they do not prove that the method generalizes beyond its data, platform, language, or user group. Network math can fail when links are missing for systematic reasons, when users change behavior after intervention, when bots adapt, or when a relation means different things in different communities. Fairness claims also depend on which groups are measured and which harms are named. Simulations of information cocoons or policy effects are useful only if the agents and feedback loops resemble real platform behavior. The family breaks when social evidence is treated as neutral ground truth rather than partial, shaped, and sometimes strategic data.

text-mining-nlp.problem_shape: This family is about making messy language usable when the words alone are not enough. The papers ask systems to judge brand safety in fiction, recover design reasons hidden in standards discussions, detect illicit or hateful behavior that is only implied, find depression symptoms in personal writing, simplify biomedical abstracts for ordinary readers, parse system logs, read privacy policies for compliance, and answer questions for different users and settings. The shared object is not just text on a page. It is text tied to time, speakers, policies, images, graphs, cultures, domains, or user intent. That makes the family broader than document classification. Each paper is trying to turn language into a decision: safe or unsafe, relevant or not, anomalous or normal, compliant or not, human or machine-written, simple enough or still too technical. The common pressure is that language carries meaning indirectly. Important signals may live in rare phrases, missing context, speaker history, domain convention, visual objects, or behavior sequences, so a surface reading can miss the thing people actually need to know.
text-mining-nlp.naive_failure: A smart beginner would start by counting words, matching phrases, or asking a large language model to read the whole text and give a label. That can work when the clue is explicit, common, and written in the same style as the examples. It fails across this family because the hard cases are not written that way. Brand risk can appear through narrative context rather than a banned word. Hate speech can be implied through coded claims. A privacy policy can sound lawful while hiding a missing limit on data use. A log line contains fixed parts and changing variables, and both matter. More context can even hurt temporal prediction when the extra history distracts from the useful pattern. The naive approach treats language as a bag of visible words, while the papers need language to be read as situated evidence.
text-mining-nlp.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is to turn language into evidence that can be compared, grouped, scored, and checked under uncertainty. A system first decides what units matter: a whole document, a sentence, a word piece, a behavior action, a label, a policy clause, a retrieved discussion, or a text description attached to an image or graph. It then asks how strongly each unit points toward a decision. For brand safety, toxicity, hate, anomaly, depression symptoms, and machine-written answers, the score is a chance that the text belongs to a risky or meaningful category. For retrieval and question answering, the score is closeness between a need and a possible source of evidence. For simplification, the score concerns whether the transformed text keeps the medical meaning while lowering reading difficulty. For synthetic text, the question is whether generated examples cover rare parts of the original collection instead of only repeating the common center. The tradeoff is compression versus detail and coverage versus precision: the system must reduce language to usable signals without throwing away the local clue that makes the case different.
text-mining-nlp.why_math_matters: The math matters because language has repeated structure, but the structure is too varied for a hand-written checklist. Words near each other shape meaning. Speaker turns and user actions form sequences where earlier pieces change how later pieces should be read. Labels overlap, so one passage can support several topics at once. Rare examples matter because fraud, hate, disease symptoms, and unusual policy violations are often exactly the cases a system must not smooth away. Domains also have their own habits: Japanese finance text, biomedical abstracts, Swahili agricultural answers, internet standards, system logs, and live-streaming chat do not use language in the same way. Scoring, grouping, and comparing let the papers reuse patterns from examples while still asking whether a new case is close enough to trust. Retrieval methods exploit the fact that a current question can be answered by nearby archived discussions. Sequence methods exploit the fact that behavior changes meaning by order. Fine-grained detection exploits the fact that one sentence or word can carry the signal that the whole document label hides.
text-mining-nlp.paper_family: The representative papers are siblings because they all repair a mismatch between visible text and the decision being made from it. Brand-safety detection, implicit hate detection, token-level anomaly detection, depression symptom induction, Twitch toxicity work, and illicit account detection all ask where the warning signal lives when a simple label or keyword misses it.
