Standards extraction, privacy-policy compliance, question answering, conversational search, and medical question answering ask a different version of the same question: which outside context must be retrieved or reasoned over before an answer is fit for purpose. BioCLEAR and Japanese financial evaluation papers focus on whether language tools work for particular readers, languages, and domains rather than only for broad English web text. VarParser and temporal-reasoning studies show that operational text carries structure in variables and order, not just prose. Cross-modal retrieval, sketch understanding, TargetMR, and graph-text papers extend the same family logic beyond plain text: language has to align with images, objects, graph neighbors, or user goals. Synthetic text and machine-answer detectability papers add a final branch, asking when generated language preserves or distorts the collection it came from.
text-mining-nlp.what_changed: The 2026 pattern is that text mining is moving from broad language understanding toward accountable reading in specific settings. The evidence emphasizes harder units: policy clauses, token-level anomalies, rare synthetic examples, speaker memories, variables inside logs, multimodal objects, graph-attached text, and low-resource or domain-specific language. It also shows more concern about whether large language models are actually the right reader. One temporal study reports that more context can degrade prediction, and low-resource Swahili answer work finds machine-written answers are highly detectable. The family is therefore less about using bigger models everywhere and more about deciding what context, granularity, and evidence a task really needs.
text-mining-nlp.limits: These explanations rest on the input summaries and the repo's current family outputs, not on full papers or independent result checking. Many claims depend on datasets, labels, and task definitions being faithful to real use: what counts as brand risk, hate, depression evidence, policy violation, toxicity, simplification quality, or a machine-written answer can change by culture, platform, reader, and law. Methods that compare text assume the chosen examples cover the important variation, including rare cases. Retrieval-based systems assume the archive contains the needed context. Multimodal and graph-text methods assume the extracted objects and links are meaningful. The family breaks when fluency is mistaken for understanding, when labels miss human judgment, or when deployment settings differ from the collected evidence.

time-series-spatiotemporal.problem_shape: These papers share a world where the answer depends on when and where something happens. The object may be ocean temperature, road traffic, vehicle power load, microservice health, rainfall, social movement emotion, sensor readings, financial signals, city activity, or online ratings. A single reading is rarely enough. The system must use the past to guess the next value, fill a missing value, flag an unusual change, or explain which earlier events may have pushed later ones. The hard part is that time is not just a list. It has slow trends, repeated cycles, sudden shocks, missing stretches, delays, local neighborhoods, and links between many channels. Space adds another layer: one road, city, service, or sensor can carry clues about another, but only under the right conditions. The 173 papers in this family are siblings because they all ask how to preserve moving structure while turning noisy streams into forecasts, classifications, warnings, generated sequences, or evidence about change for decisions that cannot wait.
time-series-spatiotemporal.naive_failure: A smart beginner would copy yesterday forward, average recent readings, or train one model that treats every channel and time step alike. That can work when the future is a gentle continuation of the past. It fails in the settings shown here. Traffic can change after an accident or weather event. Rainfall has many zeros and rare heavy tails. Microservice indicators depend on both inside-service signals and links to other services. Cities with little data need help from richer cities, but irrelevant source patterns can hurt. Long high-dimensional series become costly when every channel compares with every other channel. Missing sensor values cannot be filled by smooth interpolation when the missing part includes a peak, a phase shift, or a new operating state.
time-series-spatiotemporal.mathematical_principle: The recurring mathematical idea is to separate a stream into parts that move at different speeds, then compare the right parts rather than the whole stream at once. Some papers look for rhythms: frequency methods describe a sequence as a mixture of slow waves, fast wiggles, and repeated cycles, so ocean, rainfall, scientific, or multivariate signals can be forecast or repaired without chasing every point separately. Some papers use links: graph methods treat sensors, roads, services, variables, or places as nodes, with edges meaning that one part may help explain another. Some papers estimate chance: conditional probability, anomaly scoring, or diffusion-style generation asks what values are plausible given past evidence and what values are surprising. Others define a training penalty, meaning a rule for what counts as a bad forecast, missing-value fill, or classification, then adjust the model to reduce that badness. Many also compress long histories so the important order remains while repeated detail is discarded. The tradeoffs are concrete: speed versus detail, local evidence versus wider context, privacy versus personalization, stable cycles versus sudden drift, and smooth forecasts versus rare events that matter.
time-series-spatiotemporal.why_math_matters: The math matters because time and space contain reusable structure that a hand rule would either miss or overuse. A road incident affects nearby flow strongly at first and then fades, so Incident-Guided Spatiotemporal Traffic Forecasting needs a way to represent both reach and decay. Ocean dynamics change continuously, so KFTD uses a line of reasoning that turns complicated motion into a simpler moving state while frequency tools fill times between observations. In federated forecasting, each client has private, uneven data; splitting low-frequency shared behavior from high-frequency local behavior helps avoid forcing every client into one pattern. For anomaly detection, the useful question is not whether a number is large, but whether it is unlikely given neighboring features, recent history, or drifting conditions. For imputation, missing values should respect the energy and rhythm of the observed signal, not just draw a straight line. These structures make mathematical comparison necessary: the system needs a repeatable way to decide which past, neighbor, rhythm, or outside city deserves trust.
time-series-spatiotemporal.paper_family: The representative papers are different branches of the same deeper move: protect the order, rhythm, and dependency structure before making a decision. KFTD, GFMixer, FSDI, Fourier-Galerkin modeling, and point-to-point spectral forecasting all treat repeated patterns as something to preserve, whether the task is ocean prediction, general forecasting, scientific periodic behavior, or missing-value repair. Incident-guided traffic forecasting, Macro-Micro Collaborative Learning, SAMPLE, dynamic network modeling, and causal graph learning focus on connected systems where one place, service, field task, or variable gives evidence about another. FedRMamba, FedDiG, cross-city forecasting, and vector-injected language-model forecasting ask how to borrow knowledge without washing away local differences. DESS, DynaME, N41, ECLAD, and scalable stream anomaly detection handle the same problem from the warning side: normal behavior moves, so the detector must update what counts as unusual while avoiding memory-heavy retraining. TimeMar, Re-Diffusion, and shift-resilient imputation use generation or repair when the system needs plausible futures or missing pieces, not just a single point forecast. Even Community Notes and SMART belong here because they study how collective behavior changes around events, public events, rating flows, and display choices.
time-series-spatiotemporal.what_changed: The 2026 version of this family looks less like clean forecasting on one table and more like forecasting inside operating systems, cities, platforms, devices, and public events. The input evidence shows more work on incidents, drift, missing values, federated data, cross-city transfer, high-dimensional channels, edge-cloud latency, and language models asked to reason over time. A notable pattern is selective context: more history or more outside data is not automatically better. Several papers separate slow from fast patterns, recurring from new drift, local from shared signals, or useful source cities from harmful ones. The field is moving toward time-aware systems that must stay accurate while data arrives unevenly, privately, and under real resource limits.
time-series-spatiotemporal.limits: These papers assume that past structure remains informative enough to guide the next decision. That can fail when policy, weather, user behavior, sensors, platform rules, or equipment change in a way the data has not shown before. Graph links help only if linked roads, services, variables, or places really exchange evidence; wrong links can spread error. Frequency methods help with rhythms, but rare shocks may not look rhythmic. Federated and cross-city methods need shared patterns across clients or cities, while preserving important local differences. Language-model approaches may add context but still miss numeric temporal structure. The input file reports representative problems, methods, and selected gains; it does not prove broad reliability across all domains, time scales, missing-data patterns, or deployment conditions.
